The Tegenaria Lite is my "do anything" controller because it's cheap, wired, and I have no issues tossing into a backpack unprotected if I'm going on a trip.

Available in both Gray and White at this amazing deal price. The wired Tegenaria controller features a symmetrical design with dual rumble motors and drift-free Hall Effect thumbsticks. This controller is compatible with PC, Switch, Switch2, Android devices, and iOS devices.

The feel, as you can probably tell from the photos, is most reminiscent of a Dualshock 4, though with some notable upgrades. GameSir includes two rear paddles that you can rebind without software (or with, should you choose), as well as Hall Effect joysticks.

Despite being just $15, you get all of the essentials here for a quality controller between the Hall Effect joysticks, dual rumble motors, analog triggers, and 1000Hz USB polling rate. — Jake Roach

Googlebook software still needs some work, but the hardware is nice. Two of the nicer laptops that we tested — the HP Googlebook 14 and Lenovo Googlebook 15, are each down to $999 at Best Buy.

The HP Googlebook 14 boasts a Snapdragon X Elite processor, 16GB of RAM, and a 4K OLED display.

The only 15-inch Googlebook, the Lenovo Googlebook 15 also uses an Intel Core Ultra Series 3 processor.

These laptops are still definitely for early adopters. Still, if there's an Android diehard in your life who wants a Mac-like experience and is looking to graduate from their Chromebook, they may be interested. — Andrew E. Freedman

If you’re like me, you probably have way too many USB cables, but you can never find that fast cable when you need it. Rather than waiting until you need a speedy or high-power cable “right now” and you can’t find one, now is a good time to make sure you have what you need — or what you’re sure to need in the future.And if you’re proactive, you can snag name-brand cables at a reasonable price, rather than having to gamble with whatever randomly named wires are reasonably priced and overnight-suppable when you really need them.

Cable-matters is a well-known brand (with a reputation to uphold), and these Thunderbolt 5 / USB4 cables are rated to a jaw-dropping 80 Gbps, and can charge devices up to 240W. There aren’t a lot of devices that can push this top-tier of the USB spec yet, but when they arrive, you’ll be ready with one of these cables. Shorter options are also available if you don’t need 6.6 feet.

I typically recommend buying premium, fast cables in a different color (like red) so they’re easier to find in a tangled bundle of black or white. But these Cable Matters cables are pretty distinctive, with their black sleeves and large silver metal ends with the logo and 80 Gbps printed on them. -- Matt Safford

Most RTX 5070 laptops are selling for north of $1,400 right now, with rare dips below that price selling out quickly. That's likely the fate of this HP HyperX Omen 15.3" gaming laptop available at Walmart for $1,299, which is $1,090 off the listed price. Don't read too much into the discount percentage. This is a good deal regardless.

The HyperX Omen is a high-end gaming laptop that pairs a Ryzen 9 8940HX CPU with a GeForce RTX 5070 GPU. The specifications also include 16GB RAM, 1TB SSD, and a 15.3-inch WQXGA display with a 180 Hz refresh rate.

Alongside the mobile RTX 5070, the laptop sports an AMD Ryzen 9 8940HX CPU, which offers 16 Zen 4 cores and 32 threads, with a maximum 5.3 GHz boost clock. It also comes with a 1TB NVMe SSD.

Naturally, there are some cut corners on a device at this price with these specs. The IPS panel is sharp and fast with a 2.5K resolution and 180Hz refresh rate, though you shouldn't expect the best brightness. And the laptop comes with just 16GB of DDR5 memory, which could pose an issue in some applications, though not many games. — Jake Roach

These 1.5V lithium batteries are designed for high-drain devices and rated at 3600 mWh. The charger plugs in over USB-C and can also charge older NiMH batteries.

I’ve been using rechargeable batteries since the original Game Boy days, and they’ve come a long, long way since NiCd. Modern NiMH batteries are pretty good for things like remotes, but for higher-drain devices that need sustained wattages, they aren’t great. Thankfully, rechargeable lithium is here to save the day, and the tech doesn’t cost more than its now-previous-generation competition.

I've picked up three sets of these PowerOwl lithium batteries over the past year, to use in my smart door locks. I have had one battery (out of 24) stop charging after the first or second charge, but all others have been performing fine. In fact, they last literally months longer than the NiMH batteries I was using before. If your existing batteries aren't lasting as long as you'd like, or you haven't used rechargeable batteries in years (or ever), I highly recommend these cells from PowerOwl. -- Matt Safford

There are a million variations on keycaps (probably), but most of them look like... keys. These PBT keycaps from Hitme, however, look like dark wood — let's call it walnut. I picked this set up in 2024 after I found out that, sadly, a full set of real wood keycaps costs over $300. So while these might be plastic, it's hard to complain about the price, especially when they're on sale for just $15.19.

These PBT keycaps sport a pleasing wood look, with shine-through legends on the bottom, giving them a pretty uniform aesthetic when looked at from the top. There are caps here for 50-100% keyboard layouts, and they are Cherry profile caps.

I've had these caps on a Corsair keyboard for a couple years now and have been pretty happy with them. They look great on my living-room desk, in front of my monitor shelf with its cherry-stained wood top and drawers that I printed in wood PLA filament. If you're after something to make your keyboard look different and you don't want to spend a lot of money, these are probably my favorite budget keycaps.

It almost forces you to laugh thinking back on how inexpensive hard drives used to be. We're living in a different reality now, unfortunately, with HDD prices rising at least as fast (and maybe even faster) than SSD prices. This $150 discount on the 16TB Seagate Expansion Desktop eases the pricing burden quite a bit, offering a ton of shuckable storage space for $399.99.

The Seagate Expansion Desktop drive is a 16TB HDD that connects via USB 3.0. It's formatted to ExFAT by default, allowing it to work with virtually platform out of the box.

The drive itself operates over a USB 3.0 connection, and given that the disk inside is likely operating at 5,400 RPM — Seagate will change the drives included depending on what's available — you shouldn't expect the best speed.

Inside this chassis is a standard 3.5-inch SATA drive, so you can open up the enclosure and install the drive in a PC or server if you choose. In order to do so, however, you need to break some plastic clips that hold the enclosure together, and you'll void your warranty, so keep that in mind. — Jake Roach

If you’re after a second or third controller for your console or PC, 8BitDo’s Pro 3 is on sale for its lowest-ever Amazon price. I picked one up a few months ago at Woot, and have been very happy with it. Although you’ll likely have to update the firmware to get it to pair with a Switch 2. This premium controller gives off some alternate-universe PlayStation vibes, while delivering where it counts on build quality and feel. It also comes with a USB-C-powered charging dock that will help keep your gaming area clean (and your controller fully topped up) when you aren’t gaming.

This premium controller gives off some alternate-universe PlayStation vibes, while delivering where it counts on build quality and feel. It also comes with a USB-C-powered charging dock that will help keep your gaming area clean (and your controller fully topped up) when you aren’t gaming.

The Pro 3 has TMR joysticks, Hall Effect triggers, and supports 8BitDo’s Ultimate Software V2. And you’ll probably want to grab that software, especially if you own a Switch 2. Because I couldn’t get the controller to pair with my Nintendo console until after I updated the firmware in Windows.But after the update, I’ve been happy using the controller to play both Switch and Steam games during my downtime. And while I’m working or out walking somewhere, I really like the dock for keeping the controller charged and tidy on my desk, rather than my other dockless controllers, which just get tossed in a drawer somewhere when not in use.

Cheap and good graphics cards are rare these days, but if you're trying to save every last dollar on a modern upgrade, the Radeon RX 9060 8GB (note: non-XT) has seemingly broken free of its OEM-only status and is now available at Best Buy for $429, or $10 less than even the cheapest RTX 5060 right now.

The Radeon RX 9060 8GB (note: non-XT) goes neck and neck with the RTX 5060 for less than that card currently sells for. If you need a modern budget graphics card and need to save every dollar, this is a good choice.

Independent testing of the RDNA 4 RX 9060 8GB shows that it runs neck and neck with the RTX 5060 in many games as a baseline, and this card offers support for the high-quality FSR 4 upscaler if you need a performance boost. A single eight-pin power connector and a modest 132W TDP won't strain older builds, either. If Nvidia is a no-go for you, check out this card instead. -- Jeff Kampman

PCIe 5.0 drives were already pricey, and just as prices were starting to come down, flash demand went through the roof. Still, you can score a decent deal on the Crucial P510 right now, with the drive marked down to just $294.99 at Best Buy in a 2TB capacity. In this market, that’s an excellent price. We’ve even seen several PCIe 4.0 2TB drives more expensive than the Crucial P510 is right now.

The Micron Crucial P510 is a PCIe 5.0 drive with 10,000 MB/s and 8,700 MB/s rated sequential read/write performance.

This is (or, I suppose, was) Crucial’s midrange PCIe 5.0 offering, sandwiched between the budget P310 and premium T710. It boasts 11,000 MB/s and 9,500 MB/s sequential read/write performance, 1,500K IOPS random read/write performance, and a 1,200 TBW endurance rating for the 2TB capacity, along with a five-year warranty.

As you can read in our Crucial P510 review, the drive offers excellent performance considering the price, especially during sustained writes where weak cache can ruin performance. — Jake Roach

If you’re in the market for a tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router but don’t want to spend more than $100, we’ve got you covered. The TP-Link Archer BE9500 is currently available for an incredibly low $89.99 at Best Buy.

The TP-Link Archer BE9500 is a budget-friendly tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router delivering speeds up to 9.5 Gbps. It features an ultra-fast 10 Gbps WAN/LAN port, two 2.5 Gbps LAN ports, two 1 GbE LAN ports, and 320 MHz channel support on the 6 GHz band. It covers up to 2,600 sq. ft.

For that price, you get a tri-band router, offering 1,032 Mbps speeds on the 2.4 GHz band, up to 2,722 Mbps on the 5 GHz band, and up to 5,776 Mbps on the 6 GHz band. There are also two 2.5 GbE LAN ports, two 1 GbE LAN ports, and even a 10 GbE WAN/LAN port for connecting to a high-speed fiber internet gateway.

Other features worth mentioning on the Archer BE9500 include a USB 3.0 port for hooking up a printer or storage device, six poseable antennas, and easy configuration using the TP-Link WebGUI on a desktop or the Tether app on your smartphone. — Brandon Hill

Corsair's prebuilts offer proven, high-quality components, and they're also some of the cheapest 5090 PCs we've seen during this Black Friday rush. The latest example is the Vengeance i7600 Air. This system pairs the RTX 5090 with Intel's most powerful Arrow Lake processor and 64GB of RAM for the most demanding work or play.

Get RTX 5090 and Core Ultra 9 285K power in Corsair's Vengeance i7600 Air prebuilt PC. With 64GB of RAM and 2TB of storage, this system is ready for any gaming or productivity workload you can throw at it.

The RTX 5090 needs no introduction as the world's most powerful gaming graphics card. It's ready to chew through ray-traced and path-traced games even with 4K monitors, and its support for DLSS 4.5 upscaling and Multi Frame Generation lets you further tune your gaming experience to taste.

The Core Ultra 9 285K remains one of the top-performing CPUs for both single-threaded and multi-threaded work outside of gaming thanks to its 24-core (8P+16E) loadout, so it's a great pairing for the RTX 5090.

With all those points in its favor, the fact that this is the cheapest RTX 5090 prebuilt gaming PC we've yet seen this Black Friday season is just whipped cream on top of the pie. Get it while the getting is good. -- Jeff Kampman

Jaw-dropping deal on RTX 5060 desktop brings the price down to just $750

Finding a good deal on a budget gaming PC is an exercise in futility amid ongoing pricing crises in RAM, storage, and graphics cards. Walmart is offering a rare glimpse of hope with an excellent deal on the ABS Cyclone M Aqua, which comes equipped with an RTX 5060, Core i5-14400F, 16GB of DDR4, and a 1TB SSD for just $750.

The ABS Cyclone M Aqua is an mATX prebuilt with an RTX 5060, Core i5-14400F, 16GB of DDR4, and a 1TB NVMe SSD.

With over $650 knocked off list price, this deal likely won't last long. The major downside with this machine is that it includes a single 16GB DDR4 DIMM. That cuts the speed in half, so you'll want to add another DIMM right away. Everything else here is top-notch for the price, however. Even an RTX 5060 alone is pushing up toward $500 at this point. — Jake Roach

That PlayStation 5 Pro deal didn't last too long! Lots of people looking to get lost in Leonida. It may be worth continuing to check in.We'll keep updating you on the best deals that we find!

Look, you, like everyone else, want to play Grand Theft Auto VI. But it's not out on PC yet, so the best way to play it is on a PlayStation 5 Pro, which is often sold out and on the secondhand market for insane prices.For Black Friday, Sony is selling a refurbished PS5 Pro for $849, which is $50 off the typical price of a new one. It comes with a controller, though instead of the standard all-white look, you'll get gray camouflage.

The PlayStation 5 Pro is the most powerful version of Sony's console. It has 2TB of storage, and this one comes with a camo controller. Best of all, it plays GTA VI.

We don't often recommend refurbished tech, but this PS5 Pro is coming straight from Sony, making it relatively low-risk. It still comes with a one-year warranty. Did I mention it can play GTA VI? — Andrew E. Freedman

You may already have a KVM switch built into your monitor, as that has become a popular feature for some brands, or maybe you have three-plus monitors on your desk hooked up to your PC, laptop, or a game console. Well, this KVM deal on Amazon may help you to save some space and streamline your setup thanks to Ugreen’s 4-port KVM switch priced at only $63.99 in the Black Friday sales.

A handy KVM switch for hooking up four computers to one screen. Supports EDID emulation. All cables included except for the HDMI cables.

This KVM switch can hook up four computers to a single monitor and let you control all the computers with a single mouse and keyboard input. The switch can handle resolutions of up to 4K (UHD) at 60 Hz, with easy switching between inputs via the four buttons on the top of the KVM unit, or via the included desktop controller, which has the same four buttons, meaning you can hide away the KVM and cables and just have the controller on the desk, saving even more space.

There are many more configurations of devices available to set up via the KVM, and all you need is an HDMI cable and an optional USB Type-A to Type-C cable to connect to the KVM if you want to be able to control the device via the KVM switch. A KVM is a great solution if you only have room on your desk for one monitor, but want access to multiple computer devices. — Stewart Bendle

Kingston’s 2TB NV3 SSD is $30 off with promo code BFF588, bringing the total down to a bearable-for-the-times $265. The PCIe 4.0 x4 drive boasts speeds of up to 6,000/5,000 (r/w) and includes Acronis cloning software for backups.

A middling Gen 4 SSD with read and write speeds of up to 6000/5000 MB/s. This M.2 NVMe drive comes in the 2280 form factor and holds enough capacity to store several AAA games, and is also great as an OS drive.

The NV3 has a 640TBW and 2M-hour MTBF, so you’ll likely need an upgrade before writes take down the drive. Kingston also backs this drive with a 5-year warranty. The NV3 is great for extra storage, or you can use it as your primary OS drive. I bought the 1TB model shortly after release as an extra drive for games, and I recommend it at the current price, even if it isn’t the cheapest we’ve seen. - Joe Shields

Nvidia's RTX Spark chip launched just last month, and at least one device is already on sale: Asus' ProArt P14. Two configurations are marked down by a flat $200, including the 32GB model with the full 6,144-core GPU and 20-core CPU, and the 24GB model with a 5,120-core GPU and 18-core CPU.

The Asus ProArt P14 with RTX Spark is a 14-inch laptop with 512GB of storage. This model includes 24GB of unified memory, a 5,120-core Blackwell GPU, and an 18-core Grace CPU.

You'll struggle to run the AI models larger RTX Spark laptops — particularly those with 128GB of memory — are capable of running. However, this is still a premium 14-inch laptop with a competitive CPU and RTX 5060-class GPU.

Asus uses a 14-inch OLED touchscreen with a 3K resolution and 120Hz refresh rate. The chassis is constructed out of aluminum, and it weighs in just over 3.6 pounds. — Jake Roach

Seeing a decent price cut of $48 during the Black Friday sales at Amazon, the MX Creative Console from Logitech is now only $151.99. This is a much better price than its usual $199.99 listing. Similar in looks to a Steam Deck, this control console is designed to enhance your workflow when using Adobe products.

With 9 customizable LCD keys and a wireless fine-control dialpad, the MX Creative Console is designed to smooth out your graphic design workflow.

The MX Creative Console consists of two parts: a wired LCD display keypad with nine keys and two arrow keys for navigating between pages, plus a wireless rotary dialpad that has a central knob, a scroll wheel, and four more configurable buttons. Logitech has worked closely with Adobe to streamline software usage so that the MX Creative Console works straight out of the box with their most popular apps, such as Photoshop and Premiere Pro.

It may bear a passing resemblance to other LCD-key touchpads, but that’s where the similarities end. The MX Creative Console is designed to work with and enhance your software usage, with the aid of fine control via the dialpad. Although I’m sure you can configure this to work with a streaming setup, that’s not its intended focus. — Stewart Bendle

Olight’s IMINI 2 mini flashlight is on sale again. It’s well-designed and costs around $20 new, but it’s on sale for under $12 during Black Friday week. It has a simple design and an integrated USB plug for charging. Simply pull the USB-A port back to turn it on. The magnet on the back is great for mounting where you need a little extra light. I bought one during Prime Day this year and use it quite often when working inside PC cases or anywhere in my office where my old eyes need additional light (50 lumens). If red isn’t your color, several other options are available at the same price.

At just 2.17 inches long, this flashlight is rated to 50 lumens, and it sports a magnetic back with a USB-A plug for charging. Pulling the back off turns on the flashlight, and the magnetic back makes it easy to mount the light on anything with ferrous metal.

The Olight IMINI 2 is tiny, only 55mm long, and small enough to easily fit on your keychain as intended or even in your pocket. The Imini 2 EDC includes two silicone covers for the USB port along with a carabiner clip. Note that the flashlight portion is held to the charging port via a magnet and feels like it could fall off and get lost, but so far it has not. For under $12, this portable flashlight is a steal. - Joe Shields

After around three years on the market, Wi-Fi 7 routers have become mainstream. You can get a tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router for around $90, while a good dual-band Wi-Fi 7 router is around $75. But what if you don’t need the extra speed and capacity that Wi-Fi 7 offers, and you just want something cheap to give you decent coverage throughout your house? Well, that’s where something like the TP-Link Archer AX1450 comes into focus. Walmart is currently selling the router for $39, or 20% off its regular asking price.

The Archer AX1450 is by no means a speed demon, as it delivers up to 250 Mbps over the 2.4 GHz band and up to 1,201 Mbps on the 5 GHz band. That should be more than sufficient if you’re rocking a 1 Gbps or lower broadband connection. You get one GbE WAN port and four GbE LAN ports for connecting your wired devices. You can manage the Archer AX1450 with the usual webGUI on a desktop/laptop or use the TP-Link Tether app to control the router from your smartphone or tablet.

The TP-Link Archer AX1450 is a Wi-Fi 6 router with four GbE LAN ports and up to 1.45 Gbps aggregate wireless speeds across 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands.

The Netgear RAX5 is a Wi-Fi 6 router with four GbE LAN ports and up to 1.6 Gbps aggregate wireless speeds across 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands.

There’s also the Netgear RAX5, which is another Wi-Fi 6 router delivering up to 1.6 Gbps aggregate speeds. The router covers up to 1,500 square feet, and includes a GbE WAN and four GbE LAN ports. Walmart has the RAX5 on sale for $44.33, which is over $35 off its usual selling price.

They may not look pretty, and won’t win any throughput contests against their newer Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7 competition, but those newer routers can’t touch the sub-$44 price tag. — Brandon Hill

Best Buy has slashed an extra $160 off this MSI Codex R2 gaming PC, meaning you can save $450 right now compared to its list price. This budget-friendly gaming rig is a sure performer for 1080p gameplay, thanks to the RTX 5060, and you can pick it up for $1,099.99 right now.

A 1080p gaming PC with an RTX 5060, 16GB DDR5, 1TB SSD, and an Intel Core i5-14400F CPU.

The Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 is entry level but it's current gen, and it'll offer much superior performance compared to relying on your CPU's integrated GPU. It comes equipped with 3,840 CUDA cores, along with 8GB of GDDR7 VRAM. In practice, with those DLSS features enabled, this will let you run games with high graphics presets at 1080p without much bother.

Meanwhile, the Intel Core i5-14400F processor included here isn't a bad option for 1080p gaming and continues to be well-sold in many pre-built rigs. It has 10 cores, six of which are performance cores that deliver the best gaming performance. 16GB of DDR5 RAM and a 1TB SSD ensure no compromises elsewhere, too.

This is a good, solid gaming PC for a budget-conscious gamer, especially with that $450 discount on offer here. — Ben Stockton

If you’re in the market for a new MacBook Air, Amazon has some early Black Friday deals that are sure to put some pep in your step. You can get a 16GB/512GB M5 MacBook Air for just $1,049, representing a $250 discount over its MSRP. There’s also the same $250 discount on the 25GB/1TB SKU, bringing its price to $1,549.

But perhaps the real sweet spot in the model range is the 16GB/1TB SKU, which is discounted by $300, taking its price to a low $1,299.

This 13.6-Inch MacBook Air is complete with Apple's Liquid Retina display, 16GB of unified memory, a 512GB SSD, 12MP center stage camera, touch ID, and Wi-Fi 7 connectivity.

This model is the same shape and design as the one above, but you get a boost in storage. This MacBook Air comes with a 1TB SSD instead.

The best spec'd model on sale at Amazon right now for the MacBook Air 13 2026. This model has a 1TB SSD and 24GB of unified memory.

All of the MacBook Airs feature a 13.6-inch Liquid Retina display, the M5 chip from Apple using a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU, an N1 wireless chip for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 connectivity, a 12MP Center Stage camera for video calls, and Touch ID for biometric security. — Brandon Hill

In a market struggling with the AI boom, the best time to buy storage was yesterday, the next best time is today. That's where a sale on this 4TB Samsung 990 Pro SSD might attract your interest, available now for $699.99.

A fast Gen 4 SSD with read and write speeds of up to 7450/6900 MB/s, almost maxing out the Gen 4 bandwidth. This M.2 NVMe drive comes in the 2280 form factor and holds enough capacity to store a large selection of your favorite games or files.

We found the 990 Pro to be among the best 4TB drives on the market when it was released, as our Samsung 990 Pro 4TB review will explain, and one of the best SSDs you can buy overall. This is a Gen 4 drive offering maximum sequential read and write speeds of 7,450 and 6,900 MB/s apiece, with random read and writes at 1.6 million and 1.55 million IOPS, respectively, with an endurance rating of 2,400 TBW (or terabytes written). Our testing at the time found it rivaled the competition, sitting at the top or near the top for almost all of the tests, with the lowest latency scores (a big plus for those fast load times in-game).

4TB of storage, meanwhile, means you'll have a huge capacity boost that'll give you enormous room for a big collection of games, videos and photos alongside a typical Windows installation. The $699 sale price might not be record breaking, but it's a drop from the $800-900 range it sat at just a few month's ago. — Ben Stockton.

Snag Kingston’s NV3 1TB PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD for cheap during Black Friday week. The drive offers sequential read speeds of up to 6,000 MB/s and write speeds up to 4,000 MB/s, and 895K/795K random read/write IOPS. While this drive isn't a barnstorming PCIe 5.0 model, you'll never notice during daily use, and more importantly, gaming. That makes this a solid budget upgrade for nearly any rig.

The Kingston NV3 is a PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD that sports sequential read speeds of up to 6,000 MB/s and sequential write speeds of up to 4,000 MB/s.

As you can see above, the NV3 is a midrange-class drive and, performance-wise, sits alongside more expensive drives. It offers a whopping 2 million hours MTBF and a solid 5-year warranty with free technical support. This drive will work well as an OS drive or simply for storing your games or other applications. - Joe Shields

The Creative Pebble Pros are among the best PC speakers you can buy, especially on a budget, and right now, they're on sale for $59.49. That's the lowest price we've seen them this year.

These speakers are designed to be compact, with an angled design, running solely off a USB-C connection. Their price does yo-yo a bit, but this sale price means you can score it for a really good price: ideal if you're looking for a simple, good looking speaker setup with good audio quality.

These Creative USB-C speakers performed well in our testing and can hit 30W RMS/60W peak, though you'll have to bring your own 30W PD power adapter to get the loudest sound output.

Our Creative Pebble Pro review found these to be a decent step up in both sound and bass over the lsat-gen V3s. The duo are permanently connected, with a six-foot cable between them, which gives enough space to spread them apart. The drivers are angled towards your ears, so no need to think about stands. Connectivity, as we've mentioned, includes USB-C for data, USB-C PD for power, and a 3.5mm audio jack. You've also got a pair of 3.5mm jacks on the right speaker for a headset and mic. You'll need a 30W USB power adapter to max out the sound quality with this one, with a standard USB connection limiting you to 10W.

These are a good quality, budget friendly audio solution for your desk, so grab 'em while they're cheap. —Ben Stockton

With RAM prices still high, you'll want to find a deal that can knock a few pennies off, like this Team Group set at Newegg. For $439.99 (thanks to a $70 off promo code), you can score two 16GB modules of T-Force Delta RGB RAM at Newegg, making this (almost) the cheapest kit on sale anywhere right now if you're looking for 32GB DDR5-6000 memory if the Patriot RAM below doesn't tempt you.

Get a great deal on standalone RAM from Newegg. The T-Force Delta RGB not only adds flair to your chassis, but does so with decent speeds of 6,000 MT/s.

This memory kit is built with gamers in mind, thanks to that frosted RGB strip at the top that'll light up your case. It has a smart RGB IC controller, meaning you can control it with most lighting software like Asus Aura or MSI Mystic Light Sync, to customize it. It also has a black heat spreader with white branding.

As far as specs go, this kit is rated for 6,000 MT/s with CAS and latency timings of 38-46-46-84 using 1.35V. It's not the fastest kit around, but you'll struggle to notice a difference unless you're running benchmarks. More importantly, though, is the price: cheap kits are selling out fast, and this is one of the cheapest. — Ben Stockton.

If you travel and have multiple devices that need charging frequently, this UGREEN Nexode Power Bank is an ideal pickup, thanks to a Black Friday discount of nearly 50%. Right now you can get $50 off the usual price of $109.99, now just $59.98.

Get a 145W power bank with 25,000 mAh and a 240W USB-C cable that can charge up to three devices simultaneously.

For reference, 25,000 mAh is enough to charge a smartphone more than five times, or a laptop once. UGREEN says this can charge a 16-inch MacBook Pro from 0% to 56% in just 30 minutes. UGREEN also says this is airline-approved, although if you're a frequent flyer, you should always check with your travel provider, as regulations often differ between airlines. - Stephen Warwick

The only financially feasible way to get your hands on an RTX 5090 these days is to buy a prebuilt PC, and this iBuyPower number is now $1,200 off, making it one of the better 5090 prebuilts we've seen so far.

A powerhouse gaming PC with some of the best specs available. This rig has the 9950X3D fitted with the RTX 5090 to complement it, as well as 32GB DDR5 RAM and a 4TB SSD.

Grab $200 off with promo code BFMONTH at checkout.

The RTX 5090 needs no introduction as the fastest gaming GPU on the market, with a whopping 32GB of VRAM and 21,760 CUDA cores. This GPU is complemented by the huge AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D, a 16-core CPU with very high clock speeds and a massive 3D V-cache, which drives high gaming performance.

This is as good as it gets for a gaming PC in 2026, a true buy-it-once-and-forget-about-it option. - Stephen Warwick

This premium Asus keyboard normally sets you back $269.99, but right now you can grab this very solid keyboard at Best Buy for just $161.99, $108 off.

This 75-percent wireless keyboard features a hot-swappable PCB, up to 1,600 hours of battery life, and has a customizable OLED screen in the upper right corner.

This all-white keyboard has a distinctive look and features an aluminum top plate, hot-swappable PCB, and a customizable OLED display in the corner. There's also a matching wrist rest.

If you're in the market for more capacity, this listing also includes savings on the 2TB and 4TB models, however the 1TB version boasts the biggest saving and the best value overall, in my opinion. - Stephen Warwick

#10439. Running an AI Agent on a Local LLM: What I Measured on One GPU

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Running an AI agent on your own GPU sounds simple: point it at Ollama and stop paying per token. I set up OpenClaw, an open-source AI assistant, with a 9B model in Ollama on one RTX 3090 and connected it to Discord. Then I read the Ollama log for every request.

The agent worked. The numbers were not what I expected, though. A one-line question turned into a prompt of more than 18,000 tokens, the first reply took over a minute, and the small model sometimes guessed instead of using its tools.

This article covers what I measured and what each number means if you plan to run an agent on local hardware.

OpenClaw ran in Docker and reached Ollama on the host at http://host.docker.internal:11434. Discord was the chat interface, and OpenClaw's web panel showed the sessions and context use.

This article is about the results, not the installation. The full step-by-step setup is in a separate guide to running OpenClaw in Docker with Ollama and Discord. That guide covers the Compose file, the Discord bot and how to keep the ports off your network.

All timings below come from the Ollama log on the test machine. Ollama loaded the model with a 32,768-token context.

My first message in Discord was short: "Which model are you running on, and what is 17 * 23?" The bot answered correctly: it ran on ollama/qwen3.5:9b, and 17 × 23 is 391.

The Ollama log showed what that question cost. The model processed 18,415 prompt tokens and generated 33 tokens.

The extra tokens come from the agent itself. With every request, OpenClaw sends:

On the RTX 3090, reading that prompt took 10 seconds at 1,838 tokens per second. A slower GPU, or a CPU, needs much longer to read the same prompt.

Prompt tokens per model call, from the Ollama log. Only the first message had to process the whole prompt.

OpenClaw counts tokens with its own estimate, which was higher than the Ollama count. The gateway log estimated the prompt at 24,608 tokens, against a prompt budget of 24,576 tokens for this model. By OpenClaw's own count, the base prompt alone used up the budget before any conversation history.

The web panel showed a similar figure: 68 to 69 percent of the context window was in use for the Discord sessions after only a few messages.

The first message arrived while the model was not loaded in GPU memory. That reply took 1 min 10 s:

Reply times on the test machine. Loading the model took most of the first reply.

The speed-up comes from prompt caching. The system prompt, tool definitions and workspace files at the start of the prompt stay the same between requests. Ollama kept that part cached and processed only the new tokens. The model wrote at 91 to 96 tokens per second in every test.

Ollama's documentation says models stay in memory for 5 minutes by default before they are unloaded. After that, the next message pays the load time again. You can change this with the OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE environment variable on the Ollama server, or with the keep_alive parameter per request. A negative value, such as -1, keeps the model loaded. I did not change this setting in the test.

If you run Ollama in Docker, pass the variable with -e OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=-1 or in the environment: section of your Compose file.

Two things used the GPU besides my chat messages.

A heartbeat. OpenClaw's web panel listed one scheduled automation, heartbeat-main, which runs every 30 minutes. The agent wakes on that schedule, so the model gets called even when nobody chats. With Ollama's 5-minute default, the model is unloaded between heartbeats unless someone chatted recently, so a heartbeat most likely starts with a model load. I did not measure this.

An embedding model. During the first message, OpenClaw also called Ollama's /api/embed endpoint twice to index its memory. It used qwen3-embedding:4b, which was already installed on the Ollama server. I did not set OpenClaw to use that model; it picked it on its own.

The two models took this much GPU memory:

That is 11.4 GB for the models alone, almost half of the RTX 3090's 24 GB.

What this means for you: plan GPU memory for the chat model, the embedding model and the context, not the chat model alone. If the GPU also runs other models, the heartbeat can compete with them.

The first two tests in Discord: a question, then a file written with a tool. The user name is blurred.

The mistakes showed up when the model had to check something:

After the restart, the bot claimed it had lost the earlier session. When asked to use its read tool, it read the file correctly.

The fix for the first problem was simple. When I wrote "use your read tool to open homelab-test.md", the model opened the file and listed all three points correctly. Naming the tool made it check instead of guess.

The model listed four files and missed the test file and a folder, because it answered from its prompt.

Based on this test, a local 9B model on one consumer GPU works for:

If you need better answers, OpenClaw also works with hosted models, but then your prompts leave your machine.

In this test, qwen3.5:9b used 6.3 GB and the qwen3-embedding:4b memory model used 5.1 GB. Together the two models needed 11.4 GB.

The model had to load into GPU memory first, which took 59 seconds of the 70-second reply. Ollama keeps a model loaded for 5 minutes by default, and the OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE setting changes that.

Every request includes OpenClaw's system prompt, its tool definitions and its workspace files. A one-line question became an 18,415-token prompt in this test.

Yes. A heartbeat automation runs every 30 minutes and calls the model even when nobody sends a message.

It handled questions, arithmetic and file creation correctly in this test. It sometimes answered from its prompt instead of using its tools. When it wrongly said its memory was lost, asking it to use its read tool made it check the file and answer correctly.

#10438. Black Friday 2026 gaming monitor deals live

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's Black Friday deals time, and the gaming monitor deals are coming in fast and furious. Whether you're looking for a gaming monitor with fast response times and high refresh rates or an expansive productivity offering with a webcam, there's something for everyone. Smaller sales and events are now popping up all over the place, and we're tracking all of those sales for you here.

We constantly comb through the best deals across multiple retailers, selecting the best based on in-depth knowledge gained from our thorough reviews, extensive benchmarks, and comprehensive historical price analysis, and keep an updated list below. If you want even more options, we also have our list of Best Gaming Monitors and our Black Friday Gaming Monitor Deals hub, but we're putting the hottest deals in this blog.

Black Friday is more pertinent than ever for PC builders, as an AI-driven memory shortage apocalypse sends prices skyrocketing. Indeed, we're seeing price increases of over 100% on the most popular RAM products, so the best option could be to upgrade your monitor to a higher resolution to squeeze more gaming quality out of your existing system. On that front, we've found plenty of deals to satisfy even the most demanding monitor aficionados, as you can see below.

Gigabyte's 27-inch MO27Q28G gaming monitor features a fast 280Hz refresh rate and a 0.03ms response time on its colorful 4th-Gen WOLED display with 99.5% of the DCI-P3 color gamut. High pixel density delivers a crisp image at QHD resolution.

Asus' ROG XG27AQDMGR 27-inch gaming monitor is a flat-panel WOLED display with a crisp 1440p (QHD) resolution and a super-fast 240Hz refresh rate. Enjoy smooth-motion gameplay with a 0.03ms response time and a glossy screen finish.

The Acer Predator X27U W1 is a 27-inch gaming monitor with a QHD resolution, 240 Hz refresh rate, and a QD-OLED panel. It supports AMD FreeSync Premium and includes two HDMI 2.1 and two DisplayPort 1.4 ports.

The Innocn 2780S is a 27-inch gaming monitor with a QHD resolution, 240 Hz refresh rate, and a QD-OLED panel. It covers 99% of sRGB and DCI-P3 and offers peak brightness of 400 nits.

The Gigabyte GO27Q24G is a 27-inch gaming monitor with a QHD resolution, 240 Hz refresh rate, and an MLA+ WOLED panel. It features a RealBlack Glossy display, a 4-sided borderless design, and can hit 1,300 nits peak brightness.

The AOC Agon Pro AG276QZD2 is a 27-inch gaming monitor with a QHD resolution, 240 Hz refresh rate, and a QD-OLED panel. It supports AMD FreeSync Premium and Nvidia G-Sync and offers a peak brightness of 1,000 nits.

The Samsung Odyssey G5 (G55H) is a 34-inch WQHD gaming monitor with a 1000R curve and a VA panel. The monitor maxes out at 180 Hz and supports AMD FreeSync Premium.

The Samsung Odyssey G5 (G53F) is a 27-inch gaming monitor featuring a QHD IPS panel and a 200 Hz refresh rate. It supports AMD FreeSync Premium with a maximum brightness rating of 300 nits.

One of the most popular deals on Amazon right now, get this 34-inch ViewFinity monitor from Samsung for just $219, a return to its lowest-ever price. Comes with a 100Hz refresh rate, WQHD resolution, HDR10 support, AMD FreeSync, and more.

This gaming monitor from Asus spans 27 inches across and features an IPS panel. It has a dense, QHD resolution and a 180 Hz refresh rate, which are great specs for gaming. It also has both DisplayPort and HDMI input options.

This 27-inch Samsung gaming screen isn't much more expensive than an office monitor. But it sports a 180 Hz refresh rate, 1ms response time, and FreeSync variable refresh. It's a VA panel, which generally means better contrast and deeper blacks than TN or IPS, but viewing angles likely aren't the best.

The MSI MAG 272URDFA E16 is a 27-inch gaming monitor that packs in a dense 4K (3840 x 2160) resolution. The monitor tops out at a 320 Hz refresh rate (when operating at FHD resolution); otherwise, it's 160 Hz at its native 4K resolution.

The Acer Nitro VG270K is a 27-inch dual-mode 4K gaming monitor. It operates at a 160 Hz refresh rate at its native 4K resolution, but dropping down to FHD resolution boosts that figure to 320 Hz.

For the competitive gamers among you, you can save $100 off Acer's Nitro XV273U F5, which can run with a refresh rate of up to 1,000Hz. It's a dual-mode display, running either at 1440p with a 540Hz refresh rate, or 720p with a 1,000Hz refresh rate, and it's currently our top pick for an ultra-high refresh rate display among the best gaming monitors.

The Acer Nitro XV273U F5 is a dual-mode display running at either QHD with a 540Hz refresh rate or HD with a 1,000Hz refresh rate.

720p is hard to step down to, but 1440p downscales cleanly into it so you don't end up with mismatched pixel layouts. For most people, even the 1440p mode at 540Hz is more than sufficient for competitive play, with the 1,000Hz mode stepping in for those that can feel the difference. — Jake Roach

LG's UltraGear 45GX90SB-B OLED monitor is down to an all-time low price at Best Buy. The display is available for $999.99, knocking $700 off its list price and undercutting its previous all-time low by $200.

The LG UltraGear 45GX90SB-B is a 45-inch monitor with a 21:9 aspect ratio. It has a resolution of 3440 x 1440, a refresh rate of 240Hz, and uses a WOLED panel.

The 45-inch display has a 21:9 aspect ratio with a resolution of 3440 x 1440, along with a 240Hz refresh rate. It uses a WOLED panel, so it offers infinite contrast and near-instant pixel response times (rated at 0.03ms).

It's a high-end display with features like USB-C input with 65W of power delivery, and it features a built-in LG alpha 8 4K Gen3 processor, which you'll find in LG TVs. Running on that processor is WebOS, LG's smart TV operating system, giving you access to streaming apps, as well as live TV. — Jake Roach

My main gaming monitor is the Acer Predator X34 Xbmiiphuzx, or as I prefer to call it, Acer's 34-inch ultrawide OLED with a 240Hz refresh rate. The monitor is on sale for $649.99, a 90-day low and a great price for the display. However, the discount reflected on Amazon is deceptive. The monitor launched at $1,199, but it's sold for between $700 and $800 over the past year.

The Acer Predator X34 is a 21:9 OLED monitor with a 3440 x 1440 resolution and 240Hz refresh rate.

This is a QD-OLED panel, which provide some of the best color money can buy, and it sports a resolution of 3440 x 1440 with the 21:9 aspect ratio, and a refresh rate of 240Hz. Acer rates the response time at 0.01ms (OLED panels are almost instant in pixel transition), and peak brightness at 1,300 nits in HDR.

The one caveat with this display is the fairly aggressive 800R curve. It isn't for everyone, though it suits a 21:9 display more than a 16:9 one. The selling point for me compared to similar ultrawide was the USB-C input. Acer offers 90W of power delivery through the USB-C input, meaning connecting my Steam Deck or laptop to the monitor is a matter of a single USB-C cable. — Jake Roach

The Gigabyte GO27Q24G is a 27-inch QHD monitor with a Micro Lens Array+ White OLED (MLA+ OLED) panel. Gigabyte offers a lot of bang for the buck with this monitor, as Amazon is currently selling it for $297.47, which is a 15 percent discount.

Gigabyte states that the GO27Q24G offers a typical brightness of 275 nits and can hit a peak of 1,300 nits with HDR content. The GO27Q24G is definitely a good-looking monitor, with a 4-sided borderless design. It uses Gigabyte’s RealBlack Glossy technology, which strikes a good balance between the color-enhancing clarity of a glossy screen coating and the reflection-rejecting characteristics of matte coatings.

The Gigabyte GO27Q24G is a 27-inch gaming monitor with a QHD resolution, 240 Hz refresh rate, and an MLA+ WOLED panel. It features a RealBlack Glossy display, a 4-sided borderless design, and can hit 1,300 nits peak brightness.

The monitor has AMD FreeSync Premium and Nvidia G-Sync Compatible certifications, along with a maximum refresh rate of 240 Hz. As for ports, you’ll get two HDMI 2.1, one DisplayPort 1.4, one USB-C, and one 3.5 mm headphone jack. However, one thing you won’t find is integrated speakers.

We recently reviewed the GO27Q24G and came away impressed with its value, video processing, and brightness. As our Christian Eberele explained, “Image and gaming experience are every bit the equal of monitors costing twice as much. The GO27Q24G’s Micro Lens Array delivers tremendous brightness, as much as 1,300 nits in HDR mode. It also has nearly perfect viewing angles. Color volume isn’t quite as large as panels with Quantum Dots or Tandem RGB Stripes, but you do get over 96% coverage of DCI-P3.” — Brandon Hill

Dell has a well-earned reputation over the years for building high-quality monitors. While the company’s OLEDs have recently stood out for their price and performance, Dell also makes excellent IPS panels. For example, you can buy the SE2726HG, a 27-inch, 1920x1080 240Hz IPS panel, for only $104, which looks like an all-time low.

All-time low price.Save big and upgrade from a smaller, slower 1080p monitor to a 27-inch, 240 Hz, IPS panel with vibrant colors and high-refresh rate on the cheap.

While we haven’t yet reviewed this exact model, we know it officially supports AMD FreeSync Premium and HDMI VRR to eliminate screen tearing and maintain responsiveness for PC and console gameplay. The Fast IPS panel sports a 0.5ms response time (GTG) and covers 99% of the sRGB color space, offering vivid, detailed imagery with a 1,000:1 contrast ratio and 300 nits of brightness.

It is also a TÜV Rheinland 3-star certified display that lowers blue light emissions and preserves color quality. Connectivity includes one DisplayPort (v1.4) and one HDMI along with a 3.5mm audio jack, but it doesn’t have a USB port. It also comes with a stand, but it only adjusts for tilt. For only $104, it’s a great deal and a good way to upgrade to a high-refresh monitor without breaking the bank or needing to upgrade your graphics card. - Brandon Hill

OLED monitors have plummeted in price, and now, we're starting to see price drops on the illustrious RGB stripe tandem WOLED panels available from LG display. One such panel is available in the Alienware AW3226Q, which is on sale directly from Dell for $549.99, $150 off its list price and $50 cheaper than what Amazon is selling the monitor for on a Black Friday sale.

The AW3226Q is a 32-inch monitor with a 165 Hz refresh rate. It has a 4K resolution and uses an RGB stripe tandem OLED panel.

It's a 32-inch, 4K display with a 165 Hz refresh rate, and it comes with triple VRR certification between VESA Adaptive Sync, Nvidia G-Sync Compatible, and AMD FreeSync Premium Pro. Given that this is an OLED panel, it boasts an impressive 0.03ms gray-to-gray response time, and theoretically infinite contrast.

The display has a typical brightness of 250 nits and a peak HDR brightness of 1,000 nits. It also includes HDMI 2.1 alongside the DisplayPort connection, allowing you to run the display at 4K120 through the HDMI connections. You can read more about the monitor in our Alienware AW3226Q review. — Jake Roach

If a 4K resolution isn't crisp enough for your eagle eyes , the next frontier is a 5K display, and the wonders of modern tech have granted us 5K 180Hz panels that can double as a 1440p 360Hz display for high-refresh-rate gaming. Samsung's Odyssey G8 gives you eye-popping 5K detail and 1440p versatility for just $479.99 after an on-page Amazon coupon.

Samsung's Odyssey G8 monitor offers incredible 5K 180Hz detail and fast 1440p 360Hz versatility in one 27" display. 99% sRGB coverage and a fully adjustable stand round out this uniquely high-res gaming monitor.

Beyond its dual-mode versatility, this display offers everything you'd want from a modern gaming panel, including dual HDMI 2.1 ports, a DisplayPort 2.1 connector, and a USB hub for peripheral connectivity. If you've been looking for a way to really let your RTX 5090 stretch its legs, or you just want some of the highest pixel density around in a 27" display, this ultra-hi-res panel is a worthy and unique upgrade. --Jeff Kampman

Corsair has its Xeneon Edge touchscreen marked down by $50 across all five colors it's available in. This little 14-inch LCD touchscreen is surprisingly potent, allowing you to use for everything from a second display to a full-on productivity dashboard.

The Corsair Xeneon Edge is a 14.5-inch display designed to serve as an extension for your desktop and give you a small screen to host your most important apps. Its versatility means you can mount it practically anywhere — horizontally under your main monitor, vertically beside your primary display, or as a digital status panel inside your PC case.

Using it as a second display is straightforward enough, but there are also a variety of widgets available from the community, and you can even develop your own. If there's something you want to configure for the display, there's a good chance you'll be able to.

Corsair includes a built-in kickstand, but there are also quarter-inch mounting holes for standard A/B equipment, as well built-in magnets to attach it to virtually any surface. — Jake Roach

We’ve seen quite a few monitors on sale so far for Black Friday week, and we have another solid deal for a WOLED panel in Gigabyte’s MO27Q28G. This 27-inch monitor uses Tandem OLED technology, which, according to our review (which earned 4.5 stars) on this monitor, is “... two layers of light-emitting diodes stacked together…” Essentially, light output increases, power decreases, and burn-in risk is lower as more diodes do less work. Anything that helps to mitigate one of OLED's biggest drawbacks is always welcomed, especially if your workflow consists of a lot of static on screen items (think icons, taskbars, tickers).

Save big on this awesome 27-inch Tandem OLED 280Hz gaming monitor from Gigabyte. Originally priced at $600, this deal is hard to pass up for a premium OLED monitor and a excellent option to make the jump to OLED without going 4K.

The QHD (2560x1440) panel sports a 280Hz refresh rate, adaptive-sync, and DisplayHDR500. It covers over 99% of DCI-P3 color gamut and 84% of BT.2020 (90/75/95% for R/G/B) and 1,500 cd/m2 brightness. It comes with two HDMI (v2.1) ports and one DisplayPort (v1.4). It also has USB passthrough with two USB 3.2 Gen 1 (5 Gbps) ports. As the review states, if gaming is your primary focus, the MO27Q28G has few, if any, equals, which says a lot. And now that it’s discounted $250 (33%), it’s a steal compared to the MSRP.

Upgrade to a high-refresh-rate OLED monitor without breaking the bank. Acer’s Predator X27U W1 gaming monitor is on sale for only $269 during Black Friday and is an excellent upgrade from any VA or IPS panel, offering true blacks and excellent color reproduction.

Big savings on this 27-inch QD-OLED monitor from Acer. The Predator X27U W1 offers 240Hz refresh rate, FreeSync Premium and G-sync compatible, along with 99% DCI-P3 color gamurt and comes factory calibrated (Delta E < 2).

The Predator X27U W1 is a QD-OLED monitor with a lightning-fast 0.03ms response time to all but eliminate motion blur. It delivers vibrant colors with 99% DCI-P3 gamut coverage, VESA DisplayHDR True Black 400, and the signature of OLED monitors: true blacks. It also supports AMD FreeSync Premium and G-Sync to eliminate screen tearing. Connectivity includes HDMI and DisplayPort, but it lacks USB ports or audio jacks. - Joe Shields

The Innocn 2780S is a 27-inch QD-OLED gaming monitor with a 2560 x 1440 resolution and a fast 240 Hz refresh rate. Those are some good building blocks for a solid gaming monitor, and it’s made even better by the fact that the 2780S is now available at 20 percent off, ringing up at $279.99 on Amazon.

The Innocn 2780S is a 27-inch gaming monitor with a QHD resolution, 240 Hz refresh rate, and a QD-OLED panel. It covers 99% of sRGB and DCI-P3 and offers peak brightness of 400 nits.

The monitor offers a matte screen finish, 0.03 ms GtG response time, and 99 percent sRGB coverage (and 99 percent for DCI-P3). Innocn claims that the 2780S supports Adaptive-Sync from 48 Hz to 240 Hz. Innocn lists brightness for the QD-OLED panel at 250 nits typical and 400 nits peak/HDR. You still get two HDMI 2.1 ports and two DisplayPort 1.4 ports, along with a 3.5 mm headphone jack and two 3-watt speakers. — Brandon Hill

If you’re looking for a new monitor, Asus’ ROG XG27AQNGV is discounted by $250 for Black Friday. This 27-inch 1440p Ultrafast IPS panel has the new G-Sync Pulsar technology, said to provide even better motion clarity than the basic G-Sync.

Get an excellent deal on a G-Sync Pulsar-equipped 27-inch Fast IPS monitor from Asus. The XG27AQNGV sports dual-mode 360Hz refresh rate and 90% DCI-P4 color gamut.

The XG27AQNV sports a 360 Hz refresh rate and uses a 10-bit / sRGB+ color depth and gamut for saturated colors. It peaks at 500 nits and offers a 1,000:1 contrast ratio. The panel supports DisplayPort (v1.4) and two HDMI (v2.1) ports, plus a 3.5mm audio output and three USB Type-A ports. We reviewed this monitor and loved its G-Sync Pulsar functionality, accurate colors, and premium build quality, among other things. Making the jump to a 360 Hz panel with the new G-Sync Pulsar is a worthwhile upgrade for almost any user who isn't already using faster refresh-rate monitors or OLED already. - Joe Shields

The ZenScreen OLED (MQ16FC) is a fresh portable monitor from Asus, and it’s a great all-arounder. The best thing about it is that it features a gorgeous OLED panel that is not only vibrant and colorful, but also has the inky blacks that we expect from the panel technology. You'll also find a smidge more vertical resolution than most portable monitors thanks to its 1920 x 1200 resolution (FHD+). And you can get the monitor now for $199, a 29% discount off its usual asking price at Amazon.

The ASUS ZenScreen MQ16FC is a 16.1-inch portable monitor with an FHD+ OLED panel. Color performance is excellent, and it includes some nice touches like an aluminum unibody and a built-in kickstand.

The MQ16FC has excellent build quality, with an aluminum unibody design and integrated kickstand. Asus has you covered on connectivity as well, with two USB-C ports, a micro-HDMI port, and a 3.5 mm headphone jack. There's even a 1/4-inch tripod socket if that's a buying consideration for you.

In my testing, I found color performance to be excellent compared to its peers. While maximum brightness wasn't quite as high as the competition, it was perfectly acceptable in my home office testing environment.

High-refresh-rate gaming monitors are all the rage these days, with LG being one of the top panel suppliers in the business. It should come as no surprise that LG would include these panels in its own line of gaming monitors, which brings us to this early Black Friday deal on the 27GX790B-B. The monitor has an MSRP of $999 but is already available for $315 off, bringing the price to just $685.59 at Amazon.

The LG 27GX790B-B is certainly a "premium" monitor, featuring an RGB Tandem OLED panel with a 2560 x 1440 (QHD) resolution. More importantly, it has a native refresh rate of 540 Hz, which is already among the fastest available. But if you're willing to drop the resolution to 720p, you can boost the refresh rate to a staggering 720 Hz. If you have the graphics muscle to handle pushing out 700+ FPS and you're willing to accept 720p resolution, this one's for you.

The LG 27GX790B-B is a 27-inch QHD monitor with a native 540 Hz refresh rate, but it can switch to 720 Hz at 720p.

In addition to its speedy fundamentals, the 27GX790B-B also offers AMD FreeSync Premium Pro and Nvidia G-Sync compatibility, features DisplayPort 2.1/HDMI 2.1 ports, and a built-in USB hub (with DisplayPort Alt Mode supported via its USB-C port). — Brandon Hill

The Acer Predator X27U W1 features a 26.5-inch QD-OLED Penta Tandem panel. Acer claims that the Penta Tandem panel boosts luminous efficiency, doubles panel life, and allows for peak brightness of up to 1,000 nits (although typical brightness is closer to 200 nits).

As is typical for most 27-inch monitors these days, you get 2560x1440 or QHD resolution. You also get a 240 Hz refresh rate with support for AMD FreeSync Premium, 0.03 ms GtG response time, 99 percent coverage of the sRGB color space, an anti-glare coating over the display panel, and dual 3-watt speakers. On the connectivity front, you get two HDMI 2.1 ports, two DisplayPort 1.4 ports, and a single 3.5 mm headphone jack.

The Acer Predator X27U W1 is a 27-inch gaming monitor with a QHD resolution, 240 Hz refresh rate, and a QD-OLED panel. It supports AMD FreeSync Premium and includes two HDMI 2.1 and two DisplayPort 1.4 ports.

The Predator X27U W1 is also adjustable for height, pivot, tilt, and swivel. The monitor rings up with a 14 percent discount at Amazon, bringing its final price to $269.99. — Brandon Hill

This portable monitor from KYY is the perfect option if you're traveling but still need that extra screen real estate to fall back on. The KYY K3 is down to a record-low $55.99 right now, and it includes a 15.6-inch 1080p IPS panel with a 60 Hz refresh rate and an anti-glare coating over the display. We've tested the higher spec, but almost physically identical KYY K3-3 model, and found it to have excellent build quality.

The KYY K3 is a 15.6-inch portable monitor with a 1080p resolution. It features two USB-C ports, one HDMI port, and a screen cover that doubles as a stand.

You're getting the basics covered with this display: two USB-C ports, including one offering DisplayPort Alt-Mode connectivity, along with a mini-HDMI. You'll find that this display is compatible with almost any system, from smartphones and tablets to a PC, laptop or games console.

Despite the budget price, this laptop has two built-in speakers and an audio jack. There's no integrated kickstand, but for the price, you can always pick one up for a few dollars. As a cheap second monitor for your bag, or as a quick-and-easy second display for messages, this KYY K3 option will do the job well for less than $60. — Ben Stockton

You don't need to spend a fortune to upgrade your display, as this 27-inch Alienware proves. A 43% discount means you can score this dual-resolution AW2725QF model, capable of 4K gaming at 180Hz, or 1080p at 360Hz, for just $279.99 right now.

For competitive gamers, that's a killer choice: 1080p is still popular for games like Counter Strike, but if you're a casual gamer who wants the better visuals, you're not left in the dark, either.

This impressive Alienware gaming monitor supports 4K gaming at 180Hz and 1080p at 360Hz. It's G-Sync compatible, includes VESA DisplayHDR 600 certification, and includes a fully adjustable stand.

This model ships with Nvidia G-Sync support, so your display's refresh rate will sync with your graphics card's output to stop stutters and screen tearing. This IPS panel includes VESA DisplayHDR 600 certification, so you'll be treated to brighter highlights and more vivid contrast in games and videos.

This is a competition-ready monitor for pro gamers, but it's a friendly option for casuals, too. It has a fully adjustable stand, with tilt, pivot, and swivel options to choose from. — Ben Stockton

You can't really go wrong with the HP Omen 27QS G2 if you're looking for a budget upgrade. This is one of the best budget options for gamers that you can buy right now, giving you a decent push up to 1440p with a speedy 280Hz refresh rate, and all for just $169.99 right now.

This is a great price for a 27-inch display that our HP Omen 27QS G2 review found to be excellent, with excellent image and build quality and color that was great out-of-the-box, with a color gamut error of just 0.99. Compare and contrast to other IPS panels, which typically land around 1.7, or VA panels hitting nearer 3.

The HP Omen 27QS G2 is a 27-inch 1440p monitor with a 280Hz refresh rate. It uses an IPS Black panel and comes with variable refresh rate support.

Color performance is great, but as you'd expect from IPS, contrast and peak brightness are compromises. That said, the 27QS G2 is on the better end of the spectrum here, peaking at 470 nits in our HDR testing. That's far better than the 400 nit average you'll see with IPS panels, and it has a solid 8,202:1 contrast ratio to boot. That's better than the IPS average of around 1,000:1, but this model ships with eight dimming zones and an IPS Black panel to give it a boost.

Specs wise, this is a great 1440p monitor as a budget upgrade, especially with a 280Hz refresh rate that makes it a hugely competitive option for gaming. Price wise, you really can't go wrong: you'll struggle to find better specs for less than the $169.99 sale price you're getting here. — Ben Stockton

To kick things off, you could start with this 1080p gaming monitor from Asus. This TUF Gaming VG249QM5A is a great option for 1080p gamers with a 24-inch panel and a 240Hz refresh rate for only $99.99. It's Fast IPS, so you're bypassing some of the problems with VA panel overdrive on budget displays with this model.

The Asus TUF Gaming VG249QM5A is a 24-inch 1080p monitor with a 240Hz refresh rate. It uses a Fast IPS panel and has a 0.3ms response time.

This is a budget monitor but it's still shopping with the essentials. It offers both Nvidia G-Sync and AMD FreeSync Premium support, and also has support for Asus' Extreme Low Motion Blur Sync (ELMB) tech, which uses backlight strobing with a variable refresh rate to reduce motion blur in any fast-paced games.

The only budget compromise, really, is the stand, which only has tilt adjustments, but you can ditch it completely, thanks to the VESA mount on the back. For $99.99, this would make for a good second monitor, or an upgrade if you're still rocking an old 60Hz office panel. — Ben Stockton

Buying a monitor over Black Friday could be one of the best ways to elevate your gaming setup. In 2026, PC component pricing means that upgrades to RAM, SSDs, and GPUs are much more expensive than they used to be. Monitors, by contrast, are cheaper. So, you could spend less and upgrade your viewing experience in a number of different ways. You could get a larger monitor for more immersive viewing and multitasking, upgrade to a higher refresh rate for more frame headroom, or increase your resolution for more detail. Of course, you could also make the leap to OLED, one of the biggest upgrades you can make to gaming right now.

Welcome to our dedicated Black Friday monitor coverage, bringing you round-the-clock updates on all the best gaming monitors you can buy during the sales event. We're tracking tons of deals on OLED gaming monitors, productivity options, and more!

#10436. This Fitbit Air app buzzes your wrist with phone notifications, finds a lost tracker, more

Google’s Fitbit Air is a simple screenless fitness tracker, but it can do a bit more, and now someone has built an app that lets the Air buzz your wrist when phone notifications come through.

The era of vibe-coding has been very quickly bringing ideas to reality, and these new Fitbit Air notification apps are a great example.

“Air Relay” is the result of a developer managing to reverse-engineer a way to control haptics on the Fitbit Air via Bluetooth without affecting Google Health sync. “Cuff” uses the same method while also showing health stats if you don’t want to use Google Health.

The idea here is pretty simple. You can have apps on your phone ping your Fitbit Air as you choose. “Air Relay” lets you pick select apps and even change the vibration pattern or strength based on the app. You can set “Quiet hours” to prevent notifications while you’re sleeping, and there’s a WhatsApp-specific setting that lets you only get notifications from specific groups or people. A “Find My Air” setting uses Bluetooth strength you help you track down a lost tracker.

While a big part of the appeal of Fitbit Air is its screenless, disconnected nature, having the option to set up alerts for important apps or contacts is certainly a useful option.

“Air Relay” is free on Google Play, and Fitbit Air is available for $99.

Compatible with Google’s new charging system on Pixel Watch 4 and Pixel Watch 5, the Wasserstein “On-the-Go” charger ditches the cable and just lets you use an existing USB-C cable to top off your smartwatch. It’s officially approved by Google and works with both sizes of the Pixel Watch 4 and the Pixel Watch 5.

Normally, the adapter is sold for $25, but is down to $18.99 for Black Friday, though it does cost a dollar more at Amazon.

The simple adapter is more compact than Google’s official charging cable, making it easier to bring along for travel. It also comes with a keychain so it can easily be stored away securely in a bag, and only needs USB-C input of 5V/1.5A.

If you ever travel with your laptop, want to game on a console in places where you don't have access to a TV, or just want a second (or third) screen for your desk, a portable monitor is a must-have. And with many screens at all-time lows, veering into impulse-buy territory, there's never been a better time to pick one up. But how do you know what to buy when there are dozens of brands (especially on the low end) that you've probably never heard of (I haven't, and I've covered tech for 20 years)? Below are a few quick portable monitor shopping tips, followed by four of our favorite current deals.

This 16-inch IPS portable monitor sports a 1920 x 1200 resolution, a built-in kickstand, is just 0.3 inches thick and weighs 1.58 pounds. You'll want to get a case for it, but this is a great screen for productivity on the go.

The VE-1 isn't quite the cheapest portable screen we've seen, but I'd argue it's the biggest bargain. It's a little larger than most, thanks to its 16:10 display, which also gives it more pixels for getting work done. It's also rated to 300 nits of brightness and is slim and light for travel. It comes in different colors if you're willing to pay a few dollars more. I like this deal so much that I bought one to replace my aging portable monitor from 2018.

This 1080p portable monitor supports refresh rates up to 144 Hz, is rated to 106% of the sRGB color space, and has a built-in kickstand, a big upgrade over screens with floppy foldble cover stands.

This FHD, higher-refresh model is better for movie watching and games, as it's 16:9 and the screen is more colorful and responsive. It's rated to 300 nits of brightness and sports two USB-C ports and a Mini HDMI.

This dual-screen 14-inch setup pairs two 1920 x 1200 14-inch IPS panels in a clamshell design with a kickstand. It weighs 2.6 pounds and is rated to 350 nits of brightness.

What's better than a portable monitor? How about two in a fold-up package that you can connect to your laptop with a USB-C cable (or HDMI) and prop up with a built-in kickstand? There are cheaper dual-screen portable screens available. But most are from no-name brands and/or cost nearly as much as this one from Asus. And this Asus model has a higher brightness rating than most dual-screen alternatives.

This 15.6-inch OLED touch monitor is rated for 400 nits of brightness and sports a pixel-dense 4K resolution as well as packing its own battery that's rfored to four hours of use. While it sadly lacks a kickstand, it does come with a protective case that also functions as a stand.

Yes, the Innocn PU15-Pre is more expensive than some other deals here. But it's also a 4K OLED panel, with deep blacks, vibrant colors, and a 282 PPI pixel density that's probably better than your laptop screen. It also has a rated 400 nits of brightness that puts it ahead of most portable monitor competition. On top of that, it brings its own battery, so you won't be quickly running down your laptop's cells to keep it going.If you're a photo or video editor on the go or you just want a pixel-dense screen that will look good next to your laptop's OLED display, this is one of the best premium options we've seen so far during this deals season. The main downside seems to be that this model lacks a kickstand, so you'll have to use the included wrap-around sleeve as a stand, and those tend to be fiddly or flimsy (and sometimes both).

#10430. Kodak SlideTag is a $35 Android & iPhone tracker with an E-Ink display to show your photos and more [Gallery]

AirTag-like trackers for Android and iPhone are everywhere nowadays, but Kodak’s new SlideTag steps it up with a built-in E-Ink display that can show off your photos, widgets, and more along with being able to track down your items.

Compatible with both the Android Find Hub and Apple Find My networks, the Kodak SlideTag is a tracker inspired by the golden era of Kodak photography. The tracker is built by Reto, the same company that built the Kodak Chamera keychain digital camera.

SlideTag’s premise is relatively simple. You get a tracker with an E-Ink display and a frame in one of eight styles inspired by classic 35mm slides. Those styles are sold in a blind box format, meaning you don’t know what you’re getting until you open the box (unless you buy the full set). There’s also a ninth style that only shows up in one out of every 64 boxes.

The E-Ink display can show six-color versions of your photos, or it can display things like lists, calendars, and more. There’s enough storage on the tracker for a 12-photo slideshow, synced through the Kodak Memory Link app on Android and iOS.

Connect instantly via Bluetooth to the KODAK Memory Link App. From live slideshows and custom QR codes to countdowns and dual-network tracking with Apple Find My and Google’s Find Hub, the KODAK SlideTag seamlessly integrates retro aesthetics into your everyday carry.

Kodak SlideTag is available today from Amazon.

#10429. Best Ecommerce Platforms for Developers: Six Options and the Layers Each Leaves You

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Picking an ecommerce platform is really a decision about which layers you want to own: the storefront, the catalog and order logic, the payment flow, and the hosting underneath. Every platform below draws that line in a different place. If you have already settled the front-end question with a comparison like SitePoint's Astro vs Next.js guide, the next question is what sits behind it. Prices are from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026.

Shopify is the fully managed option. Basic costs $29 a month with card rates from 2.9% plus 30 cents, and a 2% fee applies to orders processed through a third-party gateway on that plan. Developers get two routes: Liquid themes, or Hydrogen, Shopify's headless toolkit, where your framework owns routing and rendering and Hydrogen supplies the Storefront API client and cart. Templates exist for React Router on Oxygen and for Next.js on Vercel. Plus starts at $2,300 a month.

Whop is a business platform for taking payments and sending payouts, and it sits under a storefront you have already built rather than replacing it. The Checkout element runs in the browser with no server code and no API key on the page. You pass your own order ID as metadata, Whop copies it onto the payment, and your server fulfills from a signed webhook that follows the Standard Webhooks spec. Domestic cards cost 2.7% plus 30 cents with no monthly fee, buyers see payment methods chosen by their location across 195 countries, and the same balance pays out in over 200 countries, including to affiliates or sellers you onboard. Whop's own guide shows how to integrate a checkout API into a Next.js storefront end to end. The trade-off is that there is no catalog or shipping engine; you collect address fields at checkout and trigger fulfillment from the webhook.

WooCommerce is a free plugin on WordPress you host yourself, so you own updates, security, and performance. Its payment gateway, WooPayments, charges US merchants 2.9% plus 30 cents per card transaction, 1.5% more for international cards, 2% for currency conversion, and $25 per dispute. Everything is PHP hooks and filters, which makes it the natural pick for agencies already living in WordPress and the wrong pick for anyone who does not want to run a server.

BigCommerce hosts the back end and lets you bring any front end. Core is $29 a month billed annually, capped at $30,000 in trailing annual sales, and plans auto-upgrade as volume grows. There are no platform fees when you use an embedded payment provider, and a 2% fee on Core if you use another one. Catalyst, its reference storefront, is built on Next.js, React Server Components, and the Storefront GraphQL API, and deploys to Vercel.

Medusa is an open-source commerce framework in Node.js and TypeScript, with an MIT-licensed core and a commercial enterprise edition. SitePoint covered it when it was still a young Shopify alternative; it now has over 37,000 GitHub stars. Self-hosting is free. Medusa Cloud starts at $29 a month for development, $99 for launch, and $299 for scale, with no percentage of sales, and the company says you can export your data and self-host at any point.

Saleor is a GraphQL-native, API-only commerce platform written in Python and released under the BSD-3 license. Self-hosting is free. Saleor Cloud starts at $1,599 a month for up to $200,000 in monthly sales, with 0.8% on orders above that, and $3,999 a month at the next tier. It is built for teams with a dedicated engineering function and a large catalog, which is exactly who should pay that price.

Own only the storefront, and Shopify or BigCommerce will carry the rest. Own everything, and Medusa or Saleor give you a back end you can read. Already on WordPress, and WooCommerce is the obvious fit. Already have a storefront in Next.js or Astro and only need the money to move, and Whop is the shortest path. Whichever you pick, the checkout is where disputes start, so log what SitePoint's friendly fraud guide for developers recommends from day one.

There's a new CPU benchmark on the way designed to handle and contextualize 40 years of personal computer chip development. The upcoming CrystalMark CPUix "evaluates performance from i386 through the latest processors using a single standard across past and future CPU generations," says developer Noriyuki Miyazaki [machine translation]. In terms of hardware/software compatibility, the benchmarking tool will evaluate processors as old as the i386 running on OSes as out of date as Windows 95 and NT 3.51.

Windows 95/NT 3.51以降に対応し、i386から最新、さらに将来のCPUまで、 世代を超えて性能を一つの基準で評価する新世代CPUベンチマークソフト「CrystalMark CPUix」を鋭意企画中です。 CrystalMark CPUix Project Site https://t.co/OEjTdlr4bU https://t.co/ZAfjuz6sYtJuly 29, 2026

Miyazaki says that the upcoming CPUix app will support 16-color environments, which might help folks at the more ancient and creaky end of the PC retro hardware spectrum. Even this limited color UI will have a base maroon theme, as used in the announcement graphic.

The developer is also welcoming feature requests on social media. Don't ask for support for OSes earlier than Windows 95, though, as it has already been stated by Miyazaki that stretching compatibility to Windows 3.1 "is a bit much."

To aid in the development of CPUix, Miyazaki has recently acquired an NEC PC-98 21Bs. This lovely beige desktop arrived on the developer's desk on Sunday, but it has already been used to implement and verify CPUix's functionality on processors without an FPU. Other older systems have been purchased, including a Pentium 100, to ensure wide compatibility. More systems, old and new, are also going to be acquired for testing.

We don't have a lot of information on the inner workings of CPUix as yet. Aspects of the benchmark's test workloads, score weighting, and so on aren't shared on the official pages or social media postings we found. As CPUix comes from the developer of CrystalDiskMark, it looks like it could be a more ambitious version of the CrystalMark Retro 2.0.0 release, which we reported on last year. That also supported systems back to Windows 95/NT 3.51, and CPUs from the i386 era.

CPUix is still in development, and its release date is currently penciled in for March 31, 2027. It seems to have been revealed early, as Miyazaki celebrates the 28th anniversary of Crystal Dew World.

#10423. OnePlus starts shutting down its website to ‘focus on customer support’

After shutting down its US operations earlier this year, OnePlus has quietly closed its website in some regions as it shifts to “focus on customer support.”

OnePlus announced in July that it would end new product launches in the US and Europe. Just weeks later, the OnePlus 15 and other products the brand was selling in the US were sold out for good and, more recently, OnePlus rolled out its Android 17 update to transition devices to Oppo’s ColorOS instead of OxygenOS.

Following our July 16, 2026 announcement, OnePlus is streamlining this website to focus on customer support for existing OnePlus devices. For warranty, repair, and other support, please visit our support site Click.

The same applies to the OnePlus website in the Canada, and other regions, though the UK and EU countries such as France still have an operational site that mostly push Oppo products over remaining OnePlus devices, a practice that started a few months ago prior to the shutdown. The OnePlus 15, for example, is no longer available to purchase in the UK at all. Presumably, though, the OnePlus website will shut down in these regions eventually as well.

The OnePlus website in India is unaffected and still selling devices.

The warranty website OnePlus links to appears to be more than a bit out of date, with a focus on 2023’s OnePlus Open. The most recent device mentioned is the OnePlus 13, though the page has been updated based on what we’re able to see on the Wayback Machine.
