Jensen Huang, Nvidia's reinstated CEO, has officially started his apology tour at the Nvidia offices. The firm had its first all-hands meeting since Huang's second coming, and he reportedly had some interesting things to say both about the situation surrounding his departure and the path forward now that he's back.

For those out of the loop, Huang had quit as CEO of Nvidia a couple of weeks ago due to multiple extramarital romantic relationships. The most troublesome of those is with Alice Huang, both a suspected Chinese honeypot and an executive of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which stands accused of siphoning billions' worth of export-controlled Nvidia GPUs to China.

On the all-hands event, Huang started off contrite, saying it was "the hardest company meeting [he's] ever done," and that he's been having daily therapy for at least an hour and a half. He added that Nvidia's code of conduct, mostly written by himself, is still expected to hold up. However, the New York Times remarks that the meeting "began somber before transforming into a defiant airing of grievances."

Perhaps illustrating that point, Jensen reportedly said clearly that he was not the recipient of preferential treatment from either Silicon Valley or the government itself. Some may take umbrage with that statement, given that the White House itself confirmed that President Trump called Nvidia's board himself, asking for Jensen's return, citing concerns with the stock market.

Huang also addressed his active-aggressive management style by reportedly denying he was an abusive boss — yet acknowledging he goes too far on occasion, plus that he needed to keep a high degree of dedication without hurting people.

One interesting tidbit from the meeting was that he's being subjected to a monthly 360º performance review — wherein management collects anonymous feedback from multiple people who work with the reviewee, not just their direct reports. This is an Nvidia first.

The company's board investigation about whether Huang was the target of foreign intelligence continues, though a cynical person may wonder the incentive that the company now has to complete or publish the results of said work.

#10420. Your SSL certificates can now last 200 days at most: The real risk isn’t renewal

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every SSL certificate comes with a limited lifespan. Following the latest update from the CA/Browser Forum, the maximum lifetime of a certificate has fallen from 398 days to 200, and it will drop to 100 days in March 2027 and 47 days in 2029. Renewal is no longer an annual chore. It’s an ongoing task that only stays manageable with automation.

So what does this mean if you already look after sites with SSL certificates, and will it bring drastic changes? For many setups, very little will change. For others, one missed renewal can mean an outage. This article explains what’s changing and what to do if you’re in the second group.

Today, an SSL certificate is valid for 200 days at most. The limit applies when a certificate is issued, so the ones you already hold keep their original expiration date.

Where you feel it depends on how your certificates renew. Sites on managed hosting platforms or behind a content delivery network (CDN) usually renew automatically already, often every 90 days, so the new limit changes little. The pressure lands on setups where someone buys a certificate once a year and installs it by hand. At 47 days, that becomes about 12 renewals a year.

A certificate is a promise from a certificate authority that a key really belongs to a domain, and that promise gets less reliable the longer it runs. If a private key leaks, or a certificate is issued by mistake, it stays usable until it expires. Cutting the lifetime shrinks that window, so a problem that once lingered for over a year is now fixed in weeks.

Shorter lifetimes also make revocation, the process for canceling a bad certificate, far less critical. Revocation has never worked perfectly, but a certificate that expires within weeks matters much less if a cancellation doesn’t reach every browser.

Another reason is about people. A task done once a year is easy to forget and hard to check from outside. Browser makers have pushed for years to move the industry onto automatic renewal, on the logic that a process that runs every few weeks gets tested constantly. If it breaks, you notice quickly instead of discovering it on the day the certificate expires.

For most people, the first effect is simply more work. A certificate that once needed attention every year will soon need it every few weeks. Plus, each renewal is a small chance for something to go wrong. Multiply that by dozens of sites, mail servers, and devices, and the chance of one slipping through grows quickly.

The safety nets are also thinner. If you relied on the renewal emails, nothing is watching your certificates now. Additionally, with a shorter life, there’s less time between this should have renewed and this has expired.

An expired certificate doesn’t make a site slow or dated. It makes it unreachable for most visitors. Chrome, Firefox, and Safari all show a full-page warning that the connection isn’t private, and most people leave instead of clicking through. If the site uses HSTS, a setting that tells browsers to connect only over secure links, there is often no way to click through at all, and visitors are blocked outright until the certificate is fixed.

The damage doesn’t stop at the home page. Checkouts, contact forms, and logins that depend on the secure connection fail along with it, often without an error message that points at the real cause. Other systems break, too, because apps and integrations that call your site over a secure link refuse to connect to an expired certificate.

Nothing about your site has to change for any of this to happen. A date passes, and a site that worked on Friday is down on Monday. In a 47-day lifetime, that date comes around about every six weeks.

Automatic renewal tools do the heavy lifting well. The failures happen around them:

Look at the five failures above and you’ll see what they share. Each one happens quietly. The renewal job ran, or looked like it did, and nobody checked what the server was actually serving afterwards. Automation can tell you it tried. It can’t tell you the result reached your visitors.

What closes that gap is a check that never relies on your server’s own account of events. Site24x7’s SSL/TLS certificate monitoring does exactly that. It reads the certificate installed on your web server from the cloud, the way a visitor’s browser would, and alerts you before it expires, using thresholds you choose. If a renewal fails quietly, you hear about it from the monitor and not from a customer.

For each certificate, it records the issuing authority, the owner, the issue date, the expiration date, and the days remaining, including on servers that host several certificates behind one address. That last number matters more as lifespans shrink. When a certificate lasts 47 days, the days left is the figure that tells you a renewal is overdue, and you can set your warning against it using the quarter-of-the-lifetime rule covered next.

Once a monitor is watching your certificates, the next question is when it should speak up.

Most expiration alerts are set to a fixed number of days: warn at 30 days left and escalate at seven. That works for a certificate that lasts a year and renews with a month to spare. It breaks when the whole certificate lasts for a limited number of days.

Here’s why: a healthy certificate renews with about a third of its life still left. If your alert appears earlier than that, it goes off on certificates that are doing nothing wrong, and soon everyone ignores it. As lifespans shrink, a fixed 30-day alert will start doing exactly that.

The fix is to set the alerts based on lateness, not on how close the expiry date is. Warn when a quarter of the lifetime is left, since a renewal is overdue by then, and escalate when a tenth is left. Because these are shares of the lifetime, they keep working, however short lifespans get.

The next cut lands on March 15, 2027, so a few checks now will save you from scrambling later:

Shorter lifespans won’t break your site, but a missed renewal will, so fix the quiet failures now while a mistake still costs an afternoon to fix, not a Monday morning outage affecting lots of customers.

If you’d like a second pair of eyes on your certificates, you can start a 30-day free trial of Site24x7’s SSL/TLS certificate monitoring.

#10418. Black Friday is bad for the planet. These brands are opting out

Black Friday is an environmental disaster.

Researchers from the University of Leeds in the U.K. found that up to 80% of items bought on that day, along with the plastic packaging they come in, end up in a landfill, incineration, or at best, low-quality recycling. All this after a very short time of use, sometimes as little as a few weeks. Shipping contributes to the damage; emissions from trucking spike 94% during the week including Black Friday.

The term “Black Friday” goes back to the 1950s, when the police in Philadelphia used the term for the chaos after Thanksgiving when suburban shoppers flooded the city. In 1961, the city’s merchants tried and failed to rename it “Big Friday.” In the 1980s, the retail industry tried to reconceptualize it as the day that they go from being in the red to being in the black.

Today, however, Black Friday is no longer a day. It’s an entire season stretching from late October to early December. And as a marketing ploy, it works well: Americans spent a record $11.8 billion online on Black Friday last year. The urgency of shopping these deals often leads to regret: 42% of shoppers in one survey conducted by Self Financial, a credit building company, said they wished they hadn’t made at least one Black Friday purchase. According to the National Retail Federation, retailers expect 17% of holiday sales to be returned, and roughly 9.5 billion pounds of returned merchandise goes into U.S. landfills every year.

Opting out is bad for business. Black Friday weekend is one of the most lucrative stretches in the retail year, as consumers are primed to open their wallets. But a handful of brands is choosing to take a stand and abstain from sales. Here are brands that are confirmed to opt out on November 27.

REI

The outdoor co-op first chose to skip Black Friday in 2015 with its “Opt Outside” launch, starting a national conversation about Black Friday’s impact. And while the brand lost sales that Friday, it led to a major brand boost in the form of social impressions.

In 2022, REI decided to make its store closure on the day permanent. All REI stores, distribution centers, call centers, and headquarters will be closed. Customers can still order online, and fulfillment resumes the next day. On its website, REI offers ideas for opting outside. Instead of shopping, it encourages customers to go on a hike, a neighborhood walk, or a picnic in the park. That sure sounds more pleasant than endlessly refreshing social media for new deals.

Patagonia

Patagonia declared war on Black Friday in 2011 when it took out a full-page New York Times ad telling people “Don’t buy this jacket.” This year, it has no Black Friday sale. It has a Black Friday microsite that pokes fun at the false sense of urgency the day often entails. It says that its emphasis on creating high quality gear “is an unlimited time deal that has nothing to do with Black Friday or Cyber Monday. Honestly, the best jacket is the one you already own.”

Its website remains open on Black Friday, but there is no sale. Instead, the brand encourages you to shop its secondhand “Worn Wear” collection. In a radical move Patagonia recently put its secondhand products alongside its new products on its website. And if you do choose to buy something new, it encourages you to buy products that will last a lifetime, and offers care and repair guides. More importantly, it lays out ways to give back, including its network of grassroots environmental nonprofits.

The Ordinary (Deciem)

When Deciem first went dark on Black Friday in 2019, it called the closure “a moment of nothingness” and encouraged customers to “buy less, but better.”

On November 27, the websites for all of Deciem’s brands—The Ordinary, Niod, Loopha and The Chemistry Brand—will be closed, as will its standalone stores. Instead, it will transform stores, including those in New York and Toronto, into sites for a blood drive. In its London and Copenhagen stores, it will invite customers to identify their blood type, so they can be equipped to participate in other blood drives.

Lush

Lush doesn’t run Black Friday sales. The company says its prices reflect the true cost of its ingredients, such as the organic Peruvian jojoba oil in its Gorgeous moisturizer. Instead, it has long used the day for activism. In 2016, it “switched off” its websites around the world on Black Friday, drawing people’s attention to the nonprofit Access Now. In 2021, it chose Black Friday to announce that it was quitting a number of social media channels; Mark Constantine, the CEO, said he was “happy to lose” $13 million. In the U.K., Lush stores will be using the Black Friday and Cyber Monday period to raise money through Charity Pot, a lotion that funds grassroots groups.

Freitag

The Zurich bag maker, which launched in 1993 creating bags from old truck tarps, has been saying no to Black Friday since 2019, encouraging customers: “Don’t shop, just swap.”

Since then, its online store has been closed every Black Friday, and visitors are redirected to S.W.A.P. (Shopping Without Any Payment), its bag exchange platform. Over the years, Freitag has offered fun swap events at its stores. The company hasn’t announced its 2026 plans yet, but it’s a good bet that it won’t be running a Black Friday sale.

Veja

The French sneaker brand hasn’t held a Black Friday sale since 2017 and apart from its outlets, it doesn’t offer any discounts. Instead, it has turned the day into “Repair Friday.”

In 2024, it invited people to its Paris headquarters to have things repaired by experts for free, from shoes and clothing to furniture, computers, and phones. In 2025, every Veja cobbler offered two hours of free repairs, and anyone could drop off one pair of sneakers from any brand. (Veja provides shoe repair in nine stores in Europe, North and South America.) Veja hasn’t announced its 2026 plans yet.

#10417. I love YouTube on TV, but we desperately need better watchlist controls

Managing a YouTube watchlist shouldn’t be as frustrating as it is, especially on the most-used app in my life. Google’s premier streaming app has too many issues with resurfacing content; in my opinion, this is now a major problem that needs to be fixed.

Aside from my YouTube watchlist gripes, it’s no secret that moving from a web browser to the TV is ultimately still a frustrating experience.

Lots of things I love about watching videos on my laptop or PC just don’t translate well to when I’m sat on my sofa holding a remote trying to find something to watch after wrapping up for the day. One thing I’m getting annoyed with is how YouTube scales on TV and Android TV boxes because you’re given less choice and arguably poorer recommendations for content due to the constraints in place.

Understandably, you can’t compress the layout too much on a TV as you’re typically sat a few feet away and all aspects of the interface need to be legible. I would still like to tweak it, though, if that were possible.

Maybe we could get proper sections for content, like how Netflix and other streaming platforms offer categorized areas where you can search for “comedy” or “horror”. I’m almost certain that, with Google’s insane investment and massive AI push, where every video is already analyzed hundreds of times, that wouldn’t be too difficult to do.

The problem now is that the sidebar menu is just too broad. Gaming covers basically everything. Then each line of videos accounts for one title, but requires search and previous watch data to populate. I find myself often fighting with recommendations on my TV, whereas on desktop it’s not as much of a problem.

That leads me to my biggest problem with YouTube, and it’s the, frankly, embarrassing watchlist or “Watch later” controls.

I can’t fault that it works, but right now the watchlist function is like something out of the early 2000s due to the lack of flexibility that I touched on above. As my YouTube consumption has increased 20x over the past four or five years, managing what I want to come back to or might have missed the first time around is starting to become a bit of a chore.

I’ve tried using playlists to save things, but things get messy very quickly because of how cumbersome it is to a) create a playlist on TV and b) how playlists are organized by default.

Google TV isn’t perfect, but it’s where I keep my biggest TV and movie watchlist outside of YouTube. Yes, YouTube is mostly for user-generated content, but I would take something as basic as Google TV’s interface baked into YouTube somehow. Add in categorization and auto-clear.

The Watch Later section has become an unwieldy place that I never really want to go unless I desperately have to. I’m constantly losing videos that I hoped to come back to or have an affinity for.

Videos don’t clear automatically, nor do you know when they were added. Yes, I’ll give credit that you can sort by a few options, but that’s the bare minimum. The process of moving things around is slow and takes multiple taps. Watch Later is also hidden compared to other services. It’s under your account, then beneath “Liked videos,” which is below any you may have uploaded yourself.

On a TV, the process is so annoying I just avoid it altogether. You go to the sidebar menu > Library > Watch later. It should be front-and-center on a TV. It’s almost unforgivable in my eyes because even your watch history is given greater prominence. I simply cannot understand that decision.

I’m not always a huge fan of AI being shoehorned into apps and services, but this is one of those areas that has been left to rot for a while and could get a big uplift from adding in a little bit of Gemini. Even if it were just an enhanced search function or more tools for organizing.

With YouTube TV effectively taking over regular broadcast television and being the world’s biggest streaming platform, I’m shocked by how so many areas of the platform remain in a consistently neglected state.

A little bit of spit and polish, and maybe I’ll start using this section again. For now, though, I’ll stick to texting myself links of stuff I want to watch. The ball is in your court, Google.

#10416. This Thanksgiving, let’s just not talk about AI

Maybe we just don’t talk about AI this Thanksgiving.

Of course, we need some common conversation topics to throw around the dining room with friends and relatives we haven’t seen in a while. And though AI seems to be showing up everywhere now, we still have a lot of other stuff to talk about—sports, food, movies, and the like. Or there’s always that thing where you go around the table and everybody says something they’re thankful for. Unless somebody actually says “Claude” (which is fine).

Mostly there are good reasons to avoid the subject of AI at your gathering this year.

  • Too political. Talking politics in mixed company at the Thanksgiving table can have unpredictable, sometimes explosive results. AI has become very political, mainly because of AI data centers. A surprising number of midterm voters cited an aversion to new AI data centers as the main rationale for their swing toward Democrats. Studies have shown that data centers do indeed contribute to rising energy costs, not to mention the noise pollution they produce. In fact, data centers are already so prevalent that there’s a decent chance one of your Thanksgiving guests lives near one. (You may recognize them by the way they keep saying, “Huh? What? Huh?”) Sore subject.
  • Too technical. The last major tech wave, mobile computing, was pretty easy to conceptualize. They turned cellphones into internet devices with big screens and made computer programs called apps to run on them. AI is different. Very few laypeople can explain how a neural network is trained and how it operates. Even PhDs don’t know exactly how AI models develop new skills, some of which have come as a complete surprise. That creates a problem for Thanksgiving conversation. Somebody at the table who listens to a lot of podcasts may seize the moment to nerd-splain AI to everybody. Or worse, they may go on and on about how LLMs are just stochastic parrots—word-guessing machines that will never be capable of anything more. Pedantry, jargon, and boredom will waft through the air around the table. With luck, the speaker will take the blank stares looking back at him as a signal to put a turkey leg in his mouth.
  • Too painful. Somebody at the table might own a bunch of Nvidia or SpaceX stock and get depressed. Or somebody might remind everybody that their retirement accounts are already bound up in risky AI-dependent stocks like SpaceX. Someone may gaze up from their stuffing with a faraway look and recall those simpler times when Jensen Huang was a one-woman man and everybody believed that all the AI companies buying up Nvidia GPUs would actually be able to pay for them, with nary a revenue stream to match. Heady days! They are over. Nvidia has lost 20% of its value this year because maybe bankrolling your profit-free customers the cash to buy your product isn’t the most sustainable business plan. So just don’t bring it up; heavy drinking may ensue.
  • Too personal. Don’t ask people what they use AI for. It can lead to some bad places. Just last year, a 22-year-old sitting across the table from me began talking about all the personal stuff she discussed with ChatGPT. I quickly tuned her out, of course, but there was something in there about an antifungal cream, a GLP-1 “crisis,” and a neurodivergent ex-boyfriend.
  • Too anxiety-inducing. Somebody in the house Thursday may have that soon-to-be-unemployed vibe about them, and it’s quite possible that an AI has already learned to do their job. Challenger, Gray & Christmas found that AI was the top-stated reason for U.S. job cuts through October. Soon that person will be spending their days in the uncanny valley, doing video interviews with wooden-faced AI avatars, only to be passed over (and over) by a candidate-screening algorithm that was offended by their Zoom background.

On a more serious, and more anxious, note, whether people realize it or not, our relationship with AI is pretty different from what it was at this time last year. The models aren’t perfect, or even trustworthy in some applications, but they’ve clearly become more intelligent.

We hear about teams of AI agents working tirelessly on big problems, coding agents building entire apps, and models solving some of the world’s hardest math problems. We may be headed for a world where we coexist with coequal, nonbiological intelligences that are generally as smart as humans. Discussing where this is all headed can make for an uncomfortable conversation, and not one suitable for a holiday gathering. I’d leave it be this Thanksgiving. Turkey legs and existential angst just aren’t a good mix.

The trouble is, AI has seeped into everything, raising the constant question: How is AI affecting this? So you must listen closely for signs of conversational drift toward the AI thing and have some safe, go-to topics ready to throw in. Like these:

  • Remember the World Cup this summer? Wasn’t that nice? For the first time in a while, I felt a tinge of real national pride as I watched the crowds of foreign football fans having a ball alongside Americans in our cities and stadiums. Americans got rave reviews for their hospitality—everybody from Uber drivers to hotel staff to strangers who helped our international guests get around. My favorites were those videos of Europeans discovering the simple joy of chicken tenders, pizza, and french fries slathered in ranch dressing.
  • Returning to the moon. In April, NASA’s Artemis II mission sent a crew of astronauts on a loop around the moon, taking them 252,756 miles from Earth—farther than any humans had ever traveled. They spotted a crater on the lunar surface and named it after the crew commander’s late wife, Carroll.
  • The return of the jaguar. A jaguar nicknamed “Cinco” is roaming southern Arizona’s mountains, only the fifth jaguar seen there since monitoring began 15 years ago. Researchers say it’s the latest sign that the endangered species may be gaining a foothold in the region. They also say that Cinco has a distinctive mark on its face that resembles Groucho Marx’s mustache.
  • Beating cancer. For the first time, 70% of Americans diagnosed with cancer survive at least five years, the American Cancer Society says. In the mid-1970s, only half did.
  • Fewer overdose deaths. U.S. overdose deaths fell about 14% in 2025, the third straight annual drop and the longest decline in decades, according to provisional data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

And finally, Costco’s hot dog and soda combo still costs $1.50, the same as it did in 1985. You can thank me later. Happy Thanksgiving.

#10412. The surprising — and fun — way brands are AI-proofing themselves

Play is becoming the route to making truly creative, human work. As AI makes polished output cheap, abundant, and instantaneous, brands are increasingly looking to offer expressions of character, and ways to stand apart from the inevitable homogenization of content and communications.

Externally, that impulse is showing up everywhere. Brands are lifting the lid on the creative process through behind-the-scenes content, embracing deliberately handmade visual expression and even using “No AI” disclaimers, like recent campaigns from Apple or Aerie.

Each is an attempt to signal the presence of human thought and distinguish meaningful creative work from the flood of so-called slop.

Internally too, creativity is the priority. A Marketing Week study in 2025 found that almost two-thirds of brand marketers had increased their focus on creative quality, while 63.9% rated it among the more influential factors in marketing effectiveness.

Yet striving for more creativity is not the same as knowing how to enable it. Brand managers are often asked to protect consistency, reduce risk, and deliver at speed. Briefs are often loaded with history, data, and preconceptions; teams are rewarded for control; often, ideas are filtered out before they have room to develop. And the idea of true creativity can be abstract, intimidating, and unattainable.

Play might sound unserious in that environment. But in fact, it can be a working method, helpful and inspiring; permission to experiment and make unexpected connections, combined with the expertise to select and execute the right idea.

Unlocking its commercial advantage requires leaders to rethink how they brief teams, frame creativity, and manage brands. Here’s how to get started.

Make room to play

Original thinking needs guardrails, but also room to grow. A strong brief should get teams to the point where they can begin exploring, not overwhelm them with years of history and layers of data. The best chief marketing officers or brand managers get it. They do the research in advance, then set out the ambition for the brand with a suggested set of parameters and say “go and play’”(as Chris Willingham, CMO at Brompton Bicycle, did in our recent work together), offering clarity and trust to create the conditions for better work.

This also makes the notion of creativity less obscure or intimidating. “Get creative” can feel like a loose and impossibly lofty instruction. “Go and play” is an invitation to explore. It shifts the focus from finding the right answer immediately to following ideas and seeing where they lead. The wrong idea can still reveal the right solution; rejected routes also clarify what a brand is not. Play demystifies creativity without lowering the standard. One time, a workwear manufacturer client challenged us to create something that looked deliberately “not right.” It was the perfect invitation to play, and resulted in a design that felt structured and familiar but punctuated by unusual interactions.

Play to consumer intelligence

Alongside a change in language needs to come an appreciation of a changing consumer and their needs. Brand consistency once offered reassurance. But today, the consumer expects their brands to be more animated, dynamic, nimble and responsive to the times we’re living in.   

Like people, brands can—and should—have different facets. Reliable in one moment, spontaneous or surprising in another. Wise, the money transfer platform, is a great example of a brand getting that balance right; the experience feels trustworthy, but also conversational, quirky, and human. Interactions with Wise are like talking to my intelligent, funny friend. It is an experience miles ahead of what banks like Barclays offer.

It also shows how important the notion of play is in the expressions of a brand—visual, verbal, behavioral. A brand doesn’t need to be irreverent or rebellious to embrace play. You can be one of the most serious companies but still allow playful elements of your brand to convey trust, accessibility or a more human approach. The connectivity provider rSIM, for example, offers a serious B2B product to healthcare, banking, and other utilities. But its brand and articulation are full of vim and vigor. It turns up with a unique character in a very technical field.

Embrace the unexpected

A more playful mindset also allows you to make unexpected connections, to produce the leap that makes an idea distinctive. Take the International Olympic Committee’s multiyear licensing agreement with Sonic the Hedgehog. Is it consistent with the famously strict Olympic brand guidelines? Debatable. But would Pierre de Coubertin, founder of the modern Olympic Games, approve? Absolutely. It’s a contemporary articulation of the Olympic ideal, which is to bring the youth of the world together in peaceful competition—and Sonic is a way to connect with young people around the world.  

Strategic play can uncover those connections, giving established purpose a fresh and culturally relevant expression. But it will always go hand in hand with judgment. The point is not about endless play or ideation. The commercial advantage comes from combining freedom with craft, self-editing, and the confidence to stop when the right idea appears.

#10409. TouchTunes just added a social feed to your local jukebox

The streaming jukebox giant TouchTunes wants to be the online social hub for your local bar.

The New York-based company boasts jukeboxes in more than 60,000 locations that users can control through touch screens or apps on their own smartphones. Now, it has added a “social feed” that lets users of its apps communicate with each other and see who’s connected to the jukebox in a particular establishment, even when they’re not physically there. App users can add comments and emoji-style reactions to recently played songs or share their own text posts, photos, and GIFs to a shared feed for a particular bar, restaurant, or other site with a TouchTunes jukebox. 

“We’re trying to transform from just the jukebox company to being the center of in-person social entertainment, and this is the natural next step of that,” says Scott Levine, the TouchTunes CEO. 

The company envisions that in addition to complimenting—or teasing—whoever’s playing the current song on the jukebox, users could visit a location’s feed for other discussions relevant to that spot, like planning to watch a game, recruiting players for a darts league, or sharing photos of a memorable night out. While Levine acknowledges TouchTunes is unlikely to replace existing group chats, and it’s not intended to compete with general-purpose social media apps, he anticipates the feed helping break the ice between fans of a particular venue and serving as a hub for good-natured discussions of what goes on there. 

“Maybe you have a smaller list or group of people—you’re going to communicate using message, or WhatsApp, or whatever,” he says. “But then when you’re there, you’re going to post a photo and your buddy that’s not there [will say] ‘oh man, I wish I was there.’” 

Already, the company sees reactions being posted roughly every 15 seconds, and Wednesday, when young people traditionally return to their hometown bars the night before Thanksgiving, will likely make for a test of the new features. TouchTunes celebrates Thanksgiving Eve as National Jukebox Day, and Levine says it’s among the company’s biggest sales days, at least on par with St. Patrick’s Day. 

When jukebox fans first use the TouchTunes app to connect to a jukebox after the social feed is enabled, a pop-up message discloses the new feature and invites users to visit the app’s settings menu, where privacy options include opting out of having their usernames visible in the list of people at a venue and the list of songs being played. That’s intended to make sure that users feel in control of their privacy options, even if that leads to making themselves less visible, Levine says. 

“We bring you right to the screen to toggle it off,” he says. 

But privacy experts question whether users will make informed decisions about what they’re sharing, particularly if they simply tap through the pop-up to access the normal jukebox menu, potentially while distracted—or intoxicated—in a busy bar.

“I think a lot of times people are going to be at a bar, and they want a song being played,” says Sara Geoghegan, director of the consumer privacy program and senior counsel at the Electronic Privacy Information Center. “That is not the scenario that is best suited or most apt to understand your data and how it’s being used.” 

Privacy concerns may naturally be greater for certain groups, like domestic violence survivors or immigrants, she says. They may also arise if someone encounters a creepy person at a bar who can use TouchTunes to figure out when they return or where they head next. In general, she says, tech companies rolling out new features can help mitigate concerns by ensuring that settings default to those maximizing privacy.  

“If they had the default [as] that privacy-protective option, we would have all of the benefits of the social media feed, and bringing people together, and having people enjoy music together in a shared space without the privacy concerns,” says Geoghegan. 

Still, Levine emphasizes that users can adjust their privacy settings—and block particular TouchTunes users from seeing information about them—whenever they choose. They can also report inappropriate posts that appear on particular venues’ feeds, similar to the options from other social media companies, and change their displayed usernames at any time.  

“We’re giving privacy controls on every single thing, and we’re trying to remind users, ‘Hey, you have control,’” he says. “And if you don’t like what somebody’s talking about, you can block them.” 

Some TouchTunes users appear to use usernames derived from their real names or screen names they also use on other services. But others use what appear to be anonymous strings of words or characters that would make it difficult for strangers to identify them and link them to their lives outside the jukebox. 

“The first line of defense is to choose something like, I don’t know, HappySquirrel23,” says Jelena Mirkovic, a principal scientist at the University of Southern California Information Sciences Institute and research associate professor at USC’s Department of Computer Science who has studied privacy issues in social and payment apps. “And so now no one knows it’s me, but I can still use the app and have full functionality.” 

In general, she says, app developers can help by considering privacy trade-offs, like whether information about someone’s location should be visible publicly or only to friends, and prompting users to reevaluate their privacy settings over time once they’ve become familiar with an app’s features. “Then you know people have a way to act on that, and that would be informed consenting at that time,” she says. 

Since the TouchTunes social feature is still new, it’s likely too early to say how jukebox fans and the bars and restaurants that serve them will use it in practice, versus sticking to existing social and location-sharing platforms. Levine envisions the company releasing additional tools to make it easy for venues to communicate with customers, such as publicizing specials or events, and leaderboards that could reward users who play crowd-pleasing songs as determined by reactions and likes. TouchTunes is also testing a feature that would let users dedicate a song to another user, or to a location at large, he says.  

Already, the TouchTunes app allows users to customize their profiles; they can add a brief bio and profile photo, select their favorite music genres, and even specify what they’re looking for, from “new tunes” and “pool players” to a “drinking buddy” or a “relationship.” Future versions of the app may include the ability to add other users as friends and potentially receive relevant notifications, says Levine. 

“If my buddies are all going out to the pizza restaurant down the street, and I want to go play a song for them because I know they’re there, I’ll be able to do that and join in,” he says. 

While cynics might argue TouchTunes is building digital infrastructure for conversations bar-goers used to have in person—such as when gathered around old school, physical jukeboxes with coins or dollar bills in hand—Levine argues the app can indeed help bring people together within venues, to applaud each other’s selections or offer to buy a round for someone playing fun songs. “They’re using their phones to do it, but it’s not about living in the phone,” says Levine. 

The app can also potentially let people participate in the community at a particular spot even if they’re not present, spotting photos of their friends at a particular bar, figuring out where to grab a meal or drink, or even playing a song from afar. Even before the social feed launched, Levine says he heard from a business associate who used the app to pick bars to visit, looking for venues where jukeboxes had a long queue of songs, since they were likely to be lively. The feed will only make it easier for music fans to find venues that match their wants and needs and play the jukebox once they get there, he says. 

“Users win, a location wins, TouchTunes wins,” he says. “It’s this nice, simple, synergistic triangle.”

#10406. Why isn’t AI changing career advice?

Ask a 17-year-old where their career plan came from and the answer is usually someone at the kitchen table. A parent, maybe an uncle. These are people who love them and want the best for them. They are also, in most cases, working from a job market map that is 20 or 30 years out of date.

The school counselor rarely enters the picture. Most U.S. school counselors spend no more than 20% of their time on career counseling while serving hundreds of students. The available capacity works out to well under an hour per student per year, even before accounting for group programming and administrative responsibilities.

Meanwhile, nearly the entire AI and jobs conversation is about what this technology will take away from young workers. That concern is fair. I’ve argued here before that AI will reduce the need for some entry-level white-collar roles, and employers need to plan for that now.

But we have become so focused on what AI will do to young workers that we have stopped asking what it can do for them. And there is an irony sitting right in front of us. One of the hardest problems in workforce development is getting accurate, real-time labor market information to the people who need it most. That happens to be the kind of problem AI is unusually good at.

THE DATA EXISTS BUT FEW CAN READ IT

Labor market data is not scarce. Governments, job boards, and industry groups publish enormous amounts of it every month. The trouble is that it is dense, scattered, and close to illegible for anyone without a statistics background. A 16-year-old is not going to read a state workforce projection. Neither is her dad.

So young people make one of the biggest decisions of their lives with the least information. We are preparing them for yesterday’s jobs while tomorrow’s technology sits on the phone in their pocket.

They know the system is failing them. In the Broken Marketplace, a Schultz Family Foundation and HarrisX survey of more than 5,700 young Americans ages 16 to 24, more than four in 10 said the education system and the employment resources available to them are broken. Seven in 10 said they learn about career pathways on social media.

We know that young people are already asking algorithms for career advice. They are just asking the wrong ones.

WHAT A GOOD AI COUNSELOR SOUNDS LIKE

At the International Youth Foundation, we’ve been testing this idea with a chatbot called Clara, a partnership we have with the Salesforce Foundation. The premise is straightforward: Take labor market data that would make most people’s eyes glaze over and turn it into a conversation.

Picture a young woman who has just finished a technical program and doesn’t know where to apply. Instead of a spreadsheet, she gets something closer to a knowledgeable friend. A chat that says, “Did you know they’re hiring electricians a few miles from you? A couple of things in your background could make you competitive. Let me ask you some questions and see whether it’s worth pursuing.”

From there, the tool can explain what training she would need, how long it takes, and whether that field is growing where she lives. That is the guidance a great counselor gives. But most students never get it. Nearly half of career and technical educators say their school’s counselors spend less time on career pathways than on college prep.

AI can close that gap at a scale no hiring plan ever could. Big data sets, updated in real time, delivered to one person at a time in plain language. That is what these models do best.

THE RISK AND FIX ARE REAL

To be clear, this is not without risk. General-purpose AI models can sound authoritative while missing the details that matter. When researchers at Renaissance Philanthropy tested leading models on thousands of real career questions from young people, most would have earned a C-minus. For a young person making a first career decision, a confident wrong answer can cost years.

That is a reason to build these tools carefully, and to build them now. If AI makes the labor market more volatile, good information becomes increasingly valuable. The work of measuring whether AI gives young people good career advice has barely started, and it deserves far more investment than it is getting.

The AI labs should be paying attention, too. Millions of young people are already typing some version of “what job should I go for?” into their products. Making sure those answers are accurate and grounded in real local demand would cost a fraction of what is being spent on the next generation of models.

AI can’t save every job. But it could help a young person find the next one. Employers, funders, and the companies building this technology spend a great deal of energy worrying about what AI will do to the next generation of workers. They should spend at least as much making sure it works for them.

Christina Sass is president and CEO of the International Youth Foundation.

#10405. Logging AI Prompts and Responses in Java Without Leaking Sensitive Data

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Picture this. A customer writes to your support chatbot: "Hi, I'm Asha, my card ending 4111 was charged twice, call me on 98400 12345." Your Java service wraps that message in a prompt, sends it to a model, and logs the whole thing so you can debug it later. Congratulations, you now have a customer's name, phone number and card details sitting in a plain text log file that half the engineering team can open.

This happens more often than people admit. Logging AI calls is genuinely useful, but prompts and responses are some of the most personal text your application ever touches. Here's how to keep the usefulness and drop the risk.

A regular web request is easy to log: URL, status code, time taken. AI calls are messier.

The output changes from run to run. If a user says "your bot gave me a wrong answer yesterday", the only proof of what happened is what you sent and what came back at that moment. You can't just replay it and expect the same result.

Prompts are also built, not typed. The final text is usually a template, a few retrieved document chunks, some chat history and the user's message stitched together. When something looks off, the bug could be in any of those pieces, and only the assembled prompt shows you which one.

Then there's cost. You pay by the token, so without per-call records you can't say which feature is burning money. And quality drifts over time as models get upgraded and templates get edited. Old logs are your only baseline.

So yes, you need these logs. The real question is what goes into them.

Before writing any masking code, agree on what counts as sensitive. In most business apps that means:

Names, emails, phone numbers and home addresses

Card numbers, bank details and government ID numbers

Health, legal or job-related details people mention in free text

Internal material like contract wording, pricing rules or source code

The first three groups follow patterns, so they're easy to catch. The last two don't, and that's where most teams get caught out. Keep that in mind, because it shapes the design below.

The safest sensitive value is the one that never reaches the log. So split what you record into two buckets.

The first is metadata: a request ID, a hashed user or tenant ID, model name, prompt template name and version, token counts, latency, retry count, error type and estimated cost. None of this is personal, and it answers most day-to-day questions.

The second is content, meaning the actual prompt and response text. You only need this when you're investigating quality, and even then you rarely need all of it. A sensible default is to log metadata for every call and masked content for a small sample, maybe five percent, plus every failed call.

Here's a mistake that's easy to make: letting the log appender clean things up afterwards. By then the raw text may already be in a buffer, an async queue or a crash dump. Mask first, then log.

The cleanest way is one small component that every AI log call has to pass through:

public interface PiiMasker {     String mask(String input); }

Nothing else is allowed to write raw prompts. One chokepoint is much easier to review and test than masking sprinkled across fifty classes.

For structured data like emails, cards and tokens, regular expressions do the job well:

public class RegexPiiMasker implements PiiMasker {     private static final Map RULES = new LinkedHashMap<>();     static {         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("[A-Za-z0-9.%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}"), "[EMAIL]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b"), "[CARD]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\+?\d{1,3}[ -]?)?\d{10}\b"), "[PHONE]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("(?i)bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9.~+/=-]+"), "Bearer [TOKEN]");     }     @Override     public String mask(String input) {         if (input == null || input.isBlank()) return input;         String result = input;         for (var rule : RULES.entrySet()) {             result = rule.getKey().matcher(result).replaceAll(rule.getValue());         }         return result;     } }

A few small choices matter here. The patterns are compiled once, not on every call. The order is fixed, because a card number can otherwise get half eaten by the phone rule. And the replacement labels such as [EMAIL] keep the sentence readable, so whoever debugs it later can still follow what the user was asking.

Regex won't catch a name like "Asha Raman" or an address buried mid-sentence. For those you have a few options, and they work best together.

You can run a named-entity recognition model that tags people, places and organisations, then mask anything above a confidence threshold. You can do exact replacement of values you already know, such as the customer's name from the current session. Or, best of all, you can mask at the field level while building the prompt. If your code knows that customer.getEmail() is going into the template, swap in a placeholder right there instead of trying to spot it afterwards. Knowing beats guessing every time.

Plain redaction can remove too much. If the same email shows up five times in a conversation, five identical [EMAIL] tags hide the fact that it was one person.

The fix is consistent pseudonyms. Turn each real value into a short token using a keyed hash, so the same email always becomes something like EMAIL_7f3a. You can still follow the thread, but nobody can read the original from the log. Use an HMAC with a secret from your secrets manager. A plain unkeyed hash of a phone number can be brute-forced in minutes, because there just aren't that many phone numbers.

One warning: if you also store a lookup table to reverse the tokens, that table is now sensitive data too. Most teams are better off with one-way tokens.

Free-text log lines are hard to search and easy to leak through. Write one JSON record per AI call with clearly separate fields:

log.info("ai_call",     kv("requestId", requestId),     kv("model", model),     kv("promptVersion", "support-reply-v4"),     kv("inputTokens", usage.inputTokens()),     kv("outputTokens", usage.outputTokens()),     kv("latencyMs", elapsed),     kv("promptMasked", masker.mask(prompt)),     kv("responseMasked", masker.mask(response)));

Now dashboards for cost and latency never need to touch the text fields at all. You can also keep the two kinds of data for different lengths of time: metadata for a year, masked content for a couple of weeks. Put the request ID into your logging framework's MDC so every line belonging to one call, including retries and tool calls, carries the same ID.

Streaming trips people up. Tokens arrive in tiny pieces, and a card number can be split across two chunks, which means masking each chunk on its own will miss it. Collect the full response in a buffer, mask it once the stream ends, and log that. If the stream dies halfway, run the partial buffer through the same masker.

Tool calls are the other trap. When the model calls one of your Java methods, the arguments and return values are often the most sensitive thing in the whole exchange: order details, account balances, addresses. Treat them as part of the prompt and response. Log the tool name, duration and outcome by default, and log arguments only after masking.

Masking lowers the risk but never removes it, so surround it with some ordinary discipline:

Give content fields a short retention period. Old prompt archives are liabilities.

Limit who can read AI logs. Debugging a model doesn't mean someone needs to read customer messages.

Encrypt log storage and the pipeline that feeds it.

Log the hashed user ID so you can find and delete one person's records when they ask.

Allow verbose logging in development with fake data, and enforce strict settings in production through configuration, not through people remembering.

A masker that quietly stops working is worse than having none, because everyone assumes the logs are clean. Write tests for it:

@Test void masksEmailAndCardNumber() {     String raw = "Contact me at asha@example.com, card 4111 1111 1111 1111";     String safe = new RegexPiiMasker().mask(raw);     assertFalse(safe.contains("asha@example.com"));     assertFalse(safe.contains("4111"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[EMAIL]"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[CARD]")); }

Build a small set of messy, realistic samples: numbers with odd spacing, mixed languages, addresses inside sentences, text pasted from spreadsheets. Run them in your CI pipeline, and add a new case every time a leak turns up. A scheduled job that scans stored logs for patterns that should never appear makes a good safety net too.

A few I'd watch for. Logging raw text at debug level and assuming production never enables it; debug flags get switched on during incidents, so mask at every level. Masking only the user's message while forgetting retrieved documents, system prompts and tool results. Letting SDK exceptions carry the full request body into the logs. Leaving wire-level HTTP logging on in production, which bypasses your masker completely. And treating masking as finished once it ships, when every new prompt template can bring new kinds of data.

Every AI call writes a structured metadata record with a request ID

All prompt and response text goes through a single masker first

Streams are masked after assembly, and tool arguments are masked too

Content logging is sampled, short-lived and access-controlled

Tests cover the masker, with a regression case for every past leak

Client libraries aren't dumping raw payloads into the logs

Good logs turn an AI feature from a black box into something you can actually debug, price and improve. The same logs can also expose the people who trusted you with their details. The way through is fairly plain: record metadata for every call, push all content through one well-tested masker, use pseudonyms when you need to follow a conversation, handle streams and tools carefully, and keep retention short. Set that up before launch, not after the first incident, and you get visibility without regret.

If you're going to spiff up your PS5 Pro's cooling, do it right

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The PlayStation 5 cooling system isn't an ideal design. Users report that it can run pretty loud with heavy loads and that it has a tendency to overheat easily because of dust buildup. The recent release of GTA VI revealed that many gamers needed to give their consoles a dusting or TIM replacement. But a Swiss YouTube tech enthusiast by the name of Nico wanted a more permanent fix for the issue, so he engineered an entirely custom PS5 build with a watchmaker's precision.

The final build uses a Phanteks XT V3 case, a small NZXT power supply, a Lian-Li Hydroshift II 360-mm CLC, and a pleasantly excessive number of fans. Oh, right, and there's a PlayStation 5 Pro at the center of it all. Nico shared the details of this wild custom build with Tom's Hardware.

The PS5 doesn't have a conventional ATX power adapter, but it only needs 12V power to run. As a solution, Nico split two PCIe power connectors into their respective positive and negative leads, then soldered them in parallel to a 4.5 mm cable and lug to wire directly to the console's motherboard. He wired the case's power switch to bridge the PS_ON and ATX pins, mirroring the paper-clip trick that us PC builders use. The PS5 itself then can be turned on normally via the controller.

Nico's first revision of this project used a custom loop with a pump he wired to the PS5's PWM fan control. That made the pump run too fast, though, and for our precision-minded friend, this wouldn't do.

To improve on his design, he looked far and wide and found the Lian-Li Hydroshift II 360mm LCD-C. This cooler only requires the power supply to be on to operate, and Nico particularly likes its integrated knob control, which changes the displayed information when it's turned left and adjusts the RGB LED lighting when it's turned right.

The fan sets Nico used came from Jonsbo, one of which is standard flow and one reverse, the latter of which is presumably for intake purposes. These are managed by a no-name controller off AliExpress with a remote, wired to one of the PSU's SATA power ports. He also wired the case USB-C port directly to the console's board as well.

The most significant time investment for Nico, though, were the custom 3D-printed parts he devised, namely the I/O shield, motherboard support, and cold-plate bracket. He didn't have prior CAD experience, so he reports that the entire process across his first iteration and revised builds took 80 to 120 hours to fully figure out. He expects that an experienced person would need 20-30 hours total for the mod.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

As for the cost, well, Nico says it's not much of a value. He notes that he essentially did the build twice, and estimates his costs across both builds at 800-1000 CHF, or $960 to $1200, including the value of failed 3D prints. Using his parts list and 3D printer files, though, we guesstimate that the price tag would stand at about $375 for the perfected attempt.

You can check out all the build guides for this mod on Nico's dedicated Youtube channel, though he doesn't appear to have uploaded the latest revision yet. In any event, we applaud Nico's clean build.

#10402. Driving for Thanksgiving? These are the worst times to be on the road this week

Another Thanksgiving week is upon us, which means tens of millions of Americans will once again travel by plane, train, and automobile to see their loved ones. However, this Thanksgiving period will be a little different than in recent years—at least when it comes to transportation. That’s because the American Automobile Association (AAA) says that, for the first time in several years, fewer Americans will be traveling.

“After three years of record highs, the number of travelers is slightly lower partly because of higher travel costs this year,” says Stacey Barber, vice president of AAA travel. “But travelers won’t notice much of a difference on the roads and at the airports, since projected volumes remain near record levels.” 

That means that despite fewer travelers, the roads are still expected to be packed at times. With that in mind, here are the best and worst times to travel by car over the 2026 Thanksgiving period.

Best times to hit the roads for the Thanksgiving travel period

For the 2026 Thanksgiving period, AAA expects 72.9 million people to travel to their holiday destinations by car. That’s down from last year’s 73.1 million automobile travelers, but still a significant amount.

AAA defines the 2026 Thanksgiving period as the seven days lasting from Tuesday, November 24 to Monday, November 30, 2026. But despite the expected 72.9 million road travelers, how congested the streets will be depends heavily on when you travel during the period.

AAA says these are the best times to be on the road (ie: the times with the expected lowest congestion) over the period, according to transportation data and insights provider INRIX data compiled by the auto organization:

  • Tuesday, November 24: Before 1:00 PM
  • Wednesday, November 25: Before 12:00 PM 
  • Thursday, November 26 (Thanksgiving): Minimal Traffic Impact Expected 
  • Friday, November 27: Before 12:00 PM 
  • Saturday, November 28: Before 11:00 AM 
  • Sunday, November 29: Before 11:00 AM 
  • Monday, November 30: Before 1:00 PM 

Worst times to hit the roads for the Thanksgiving travel period

INRIX data shows that the worst days to travel over the Thanksgiving period—that is, the days the congestion is expected to be the highest—are the Tuesday and Wednesday before Thanksgiving, and the Sunday and Monday after. Those are the days when most people choose to travel to and from their holiday destinations.

As for the individual times that are expected to be the worst to travel by car, those are:

  • Tuesday, November 24: 2:00 PM to 8:00 PM 
  • Wednesday, November 25: 12:00 PM to 7:00 PM 
  • Thursday, November 26 (Thanksgiving): Minimal Traffic Impact Expected 
  • Friday, November 27: 1:00 PM to 7:00 PM 
  • Saturday, November 28: 12:00 PM to 9:00 PM 
  • Sunday, November 29: 12:00 PM to 8:00 PM 
  • Monday, November 30: 2:00 PM to 7:00 PM 

Fewer total travelers are expected over the Thanksgiving 2026 period

When combining all modes of transportation—auto, air, and “other,” which includes bus, boat, and train—AAA says 81.48 million people in America are expected to travel over the 2026 Thanksgiving period.

That’s about 121,000 fewer than the 81.61 million who traveled during the 2025 Thanksgiving period. Still, 2026’s expected numbers far surpass the 77.78 million people who traveled in 2019, the last year before the pandemic.

The expected decline in travelers this year is mainly due to higher travel costs, especially gas prices, AAA says. 

Besides a decline of about 200,000 car travelers, AAA says there will also be a drop in air travelers by about 0.2% to 5.96 million (versus 5.97 million in 2025). 

However, more people will travel by “other” modes during this period than last year. “Other” includes travel by bus, train, and cruise.

In the 2026 Thanksgiving period, the other travel segment is expected to reach 2.6 million travelers—up 4.1% from 2.49 million in 2025.

#10400. 6 tips to use this Thanksgiving when family asks about your career

Evan Reece has a few strategies for handling unwelcome questions about his career when he gathers with family. He founded and ran a ski lift ticket platform for 15 years, but it went out of business during the COVID-19 pandemic. Reece then started a career management platform. He’s its sole employee and earns less than he did before.

At family parties, he sometimes feels pressure to explain why he doesn’t get a full-time job working for someone else. When he’s asked such questions, he reminds himself that people usually ask because they care.

“Oftentimes, if we’re stressed about something that we don’t have an answer to, the question feels like an interrogation, when that’s rarely the intention of the person asking the question,” said Reece, 48, who runs the career management platform Truest.me.

A simple “How’s your job going?” can feel like an ambush when you’re unemployed, underemployed or working in jobs your friends and relatives don’t understand or may regard as frivolous. These queries can bring up painful experiences like layoffs. Advice can sound like criticism to recent graduates in a seemingly impenetrable job market, while curiosity about someone’s income can feel like judgment.

Even inquiries motivated by a genuine desire to connect can come across as invasive or awkward in a group setting.

With holiday gatherings approaching, here are some tips and potential scripts to help you handle tricky career conversations with relatives and feel less defensive. The same strategies can be applied when faced with scrutiny about getting married or having children.

Anticipate questions and plan responses in advance

Have a short, confident response or two ready for the job-related queries you think might come up, said Melody Wilding, an executive coach and author of “Managing Up.”

For example, if you’re unemployed, you could say, “I’m taking time to find the right fit and not rushing into something new.” Or if you’ve made an unconventional career move, say, “I know it’s not what everyone would choose, but I’m excited about it,” Wilding said.

“Then redirect the conversation nicely. You might say, ‘Tell me about you,’ or ‘I’d love to hear about your recent trip,'” she added.

Be a boomerang when fielding questions

Turning the inquiries around on the questioner can deflect attention and be entertaining.

“If someone is willing to ask you a question that requires tremendous vulnerability out of you, then they should be willing to answer one too,” Reece said.

When a relative asks if you’re “still job searching” or “Why did you leave a good job?” get curious before you get defensive, Wilding suggested. Instead of immediately responding to their question, try to understand the motivation behind it by countering, “Why do you ask?” or “What makes you say that?” Wilding said.

“Maybe they’re just making conversation, which saves you from launching into a full defense of your choices,” she said.

Turn it into a game

If someone asks about an unstable job or recent layoff, you can say it’s been challenging and then suggest, “Let’s play a game. Everybody tell a story about the worst job they ever had,” Reece said. “Anybody who’s ever worked has a story. And they’re usually amazing.”

For recent graduates or those who are trying to figure out what’s next, you could be honest about your uncertainty and reply, “Everybody go around and talk about a time in their career when they weren’t sure what to do next and what you did,” Reece suggested.

Let others take the spotlight

Hope Bond, 53, spent a decade working as an editor in the magazine industry. She left the field for a few years to raise her young children, then did some freelance editing jobs. When she sought to return to full-time work in 2020, she couldn’t find a position. Bond began working as a site manager for a movie production location in 2024.

She loves the job, despite its erratic hours, instability and hourly pay. But at gatherings with her family of lawyers and bankers, she often felt singled out by probing questions about her work.

After years of answering their questions, she now redirects them and encourages others to be the star of the conversation, especially her children.

“I stay on the periphery. The younger generations are the ones who are bringing the great energy, so I like them to have the floor,” Bond said. “I don’t insert myself into conversation if we’re talking about career or money. Those are my two boundaries. Even with a family that is loving and supportive and wants the best for me, it is just awkward.”

Share context about the job market

When people feel scrutinized after layoffs or extended unemployment, Avigail Lev, a psychologist at the Bay Area CBT Center in San Francisco, suggests explaining to family members how the job market has changed and how artificial intelligence has impacted their fields.

“The first thing you need to say is to speak to the context that things are different, and the decisions about work are very different right now,” Lev said.

Many of Lev’s clients work in technology or at AI companies and worry about losing their jobs, while some have already been laid off, she said.

“Some people are very depressed right now about not having work or not knowing what’s next. And having a relative blame you for something that’s not in your control is the last thing that you need right now,” Lev said.

Choose what you reveal

One way to avoid unnecessary judgment is to choose whom you share details about your professional life with.

Rishabh Dutta, 25, of Mumbai, India, quit his marketing job for Bollywood movies after stress and long hours led to hair loss. For the next few months, “everyone was constantly asking me what I was doing, if I had found something else,” he said.

The next time Dutta left a job, he kept it to himself for a few months. “I just decided not to tell them, and honestly I don’t regret it,” he said.

Share your stories and questions about workplace wellness at cbussewitz@ap.org. Follow AP’s Be Well coverage, focusing on wellness, fitness, diet and mental health at https://apnews.com/hub/be-well.

—Cathy Bussewitz, AP Business Writer

#10397. The 10-person board that voted to reinstate Nvidia’s CEO is also now under scrutiny

Jensen Huang has been under a spotlight for weeks, but after the 11-day period of disorder that included the resignation and reinstatement of the Nvidia executive, the company’s board is joining him at the center of scrutiny.

The 10-person board voted unanimously to rehire Huang as Nvidia’s president, CEO and a fellow board member, writing in an announcement Monday that the decision emerged after discussions with Huang and “input from senior levels of the United States government.” President Donald Trump said he believes his intervention was crucial to the reinstatement.

Just six days earlier, the board was singing a different tune. Board members had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation following his admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The board did not intend to reinstate him, Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of a quarterly earnings call.

“To bow to pressure to bring someone back who has hurt the reputation of the company is crazy,” said Kathleen Day, a lecturer at Johns Hopkins Carey Business School.

The board’s stunning reversal has spurred questions about its independence and what Trump’s role means for the meeting of business and politics.

Concerns swirl about corporate governance and Trump’s intervention

Nvidia’s board includes both business leaders with longstanding ties to the company and a group of more recent additions who have experience at big-name companies including Taco Bell, PepsiCo and Eli Lilly.

Some experts have called for the board to resign in the wake of the havoc.

Day, who has expertise in financial crises and corporate governance, emphasized that the board has a duty to represent shareholders, not the CEO.

“The shareholders should demand a new board,” she said.

Corporate governance experts say long tenures for board members can compromise their independence. Under the rules of the New York Stock Exchange and the Nasdaq, companies are required to have a majority of directors who are independent.

“Traditionally, it’s a good practice” to limit how long people can sit on a board, said Nada Kakabadse, professor of policy, governance and ethics at the University of Reading’s Henley Business School. “They should be eight years maximum. Four years, plus another four years if they’re performing well. But beyond that, they really become not independent anymore, right?”

It’s not unusual for U.S. tech bosses to stuff their boards with allies or high-profile figures who might not be aware of what’s happening at the company, Kakabadse said.

American business has a culture of “leader heroes” — entrepreneurs who founded companies and are seen as the only ones who can steer them through tough times, she said. But at some point, the companies can get so big that “you need proper corporate structure, you need proper governance.”

Many people are also questioning what “input” the company received from senior government leaders and why it persuaded the board to make a complete turnaround.

“The board should have listened to the president’s request and stuck to its position that it was time to find a new CEO,” said Peter Cohan, an associate professor of management practice at Babson College. “In my opinion, by giving in to Trump, the board is endangering the company. That’s because Huang has seen that he can do anything he wants, and he will get away with it.”

The idea of an independent board of experts looking out for the long-term interests of the company and its shareholders “sort of goes out the window” if the sitting president “essentially tells them what to do,” said Daniel Kinderman, a professor of political science and international relations at the University of Delaware.

“This is really the mark of crony capitalism, right?” he said.

Kinderman said the episode might “open the door a little bit more for more aggressive actions on behalf of elected representatives” in their relationships with businesses.

Lawmakers call for accountability from the board

The Nvidia saga has made waves in Washington, particularly in conversations around export controls. Huang’s affair raised questions about Nvidia’s compliance with those restrictions. The reinstatement has renewed fervor on Capitol Hill for more transparency from both Huang and the board.

Elected officials from both parties were quick to respond to the reinstatement with criticism and skepticism.

Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, said the decision to bring Huang back was “reckless.” She wrote in a statement Monday that it does not change the fact that Huang, Nvidia executives and the company’s board “still owe Congress answers.”

Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, a New York Democrat, called for both Huang and the board to testify publicly to Congress. “A boardroom vote does not resolve a national security risk,” she said in a statement Monday.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who is investigating Nvidia in connection with Huang’s affair, said Tuesday in an interview with CNBC that the president’s intervention “does not bode well for enforcement of the law by the federal government without fear, without favor.”

The California Department of Justice said Thursday that it is asking Nvidia whether its advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China and whether Nvidia misled investors and the public.

Some members joined the Nvidia board in the 1990s

Two board members, Mark Stevens and Tench Coxe, joined the board in 1993 when Nvidia was founded. Stevens and Coxe were both previously venture capitalists who made early investments in Nvidia.

Two other long-serving board members, Jones and Brooke Seawell, are the former chief executive and chief financial officer, respectively, of Synopsys, which makes chip-design software and counted Nvidia as its first customer. Jones joined Nvidia’s board in 1993, while Seawell joined four years later.

Stephen Neal, who’s designated as the board’s “lead independent director,” joined in 2019. He’s the chairman emeritus of Cooley LLP, Nvidia’s longtime law firm, and has advised the company in “various governance matters,” according to his bio.

Other board members have less of a direct link to Nvidia.

Melissa Lora, former president of Taco Bell International, spent 31 years at the fast food company and joined Nvidia’s board in 2023. Aarti Shah, formerly a senior vice president and chief digital officer at pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly, joined in 2020.

John Dabiri, an engineering professor at the California Institute of Technology whose lab researches fluid mechanics, was added to the board in 2020. Dawn Hudson was the NFL’s chief marketing officer and a former CEO of Pepsi-Cola’s North American division who’s been on the board since 2013. Suzanne Nora Johnson was a vice chairman at Goldman Sachs who joined the board in July.

None of the board members provided comment in response to requests from The Associated Press.

This story corrects that Shah joined the Nvidia board in 2020, not 2021.

—Kaitlyn Huamani and Kelvin Chan, Associated Press

#10393. Digital Duty of Care Act passes in Australia. Opposition say the law is ‘authoritarian’

Australia’s Parliament on Wednesday passed online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms.

The United States and the Australian opposition party warned that the legislation would lead to censorship of lawful speech.

The Digital Duty of Care Act requires Big Tech to proactively reduce the risk of harm before it occurs, according to an Australian government statement.

Australian online law falls in line with EU and British legislation

The legislation is similar to the European Union’s Digital Services Act, passed in 2022, and the United Kingdom’s Online Safety Act passed a year later.

The legislation became law in the House of Representatives, where the center-left Labor Party government commands a majority, by 97 votes to 43.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told Parliament the law would stand as a “powerful instrument to protect our children and our society from online harms by placing the onus on the tech platforms to ensure a safer online environment.”

“This is a victory for our children and young people. The dangers were unforeseen when the digital world was young,” Albanese said. “But now that the digital world has matured, they can be easily recognized and they can be remedied.”

Opposition leader vows to repeal ‘authoritarian’ law

Opposition leader Angus Taylor told Parliament he would repeal the legislation if his conservative Liberal Party wins elections in 2028. Taylor described the legislation as “authoritarian.”

“This bill is a blank check for political censorship,” Taylor told Parliament. “The bill is an attack on free speech that is absolutely central to our democracy.”

The government struck a deal with the minor Greens party on Tuesday to get the legislation through the Senate, where no party holds a majority.

“Today, the safety and wellbeing of Australians and their children have finally been put ahead of Big Tech’s bottom line,” Greens chief negotiator Sarah Hanson-Young said in a statement after the bill passed the Senate by 36 votes to 23.

“My message to Big Tech companies is, it’s time to make your platforms safe or we will see you in court,” she added.

The Australian legislation sets minimum safety standards for online services, including games, apps and artificial intelligence chatbots, requiring them to protect Australians from seriously harmful material and conduct, the government said.

The Greens’ amendments include increasing maximum penalties for breaches from 109 million Australian dollars ($72 million), as the government originally proposed, to 5% of a tech company’s global revenue.

U.S. Ambassador to Australia David Brat said on Tuesday the then-proposed laws would “impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors.”

“Vaguely defined ‘harms,’ backed by penalties of up to 5% of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech,” Brat posted on social media.

—Rod Mcguirk, Associated Press
